## Layer 5: Arithmetic and quantum connections

This layer connects the analytic theory with arithmetic and topology at the boundary of ℍ. It defines radial limits and radial asymptotic expansions at rational points, derives them from Euler–Maclaurin and Mellin transforms, and defines Zagier's quantum modular forms with their period cocycles. Eichler integrals of half-integral-weight cusp forms are quantum modular (Bringmann–Rolen); Kontsevich's strange function, compared with the Habiro element of HabiroCyclotomicCompletions, is quantum modular of weight 3/2 through Zagier's strange identity; the WRT invariants of the Poincaré sphere are radial limits of the Lawrence–Zagier series and form a quantum modular form. The crank and the rank explain Ramanujan's congruences, including the one modulo 11, and their radial limits at roots of unity are values of unimodal series (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades). The last subsection proves Zagier's theorem that the traces of singular moduli are the coefficients of a weight-3/2 form.

Standing assumptions: rational points x = h/k are in lowest terms; q → ζ radially means q = ζe^{−t}, t ↓ 0; Habiro evaluations and radial limits are distinct objects compared by explicit theorems.

### 5.1 Radial limits and asymptotic expansions

**Radial limits at rational points and at roots of unity.** Define `HasRadialLimit`. For a function G : ℂ → ℂ (only its values on the upper half-plane ℍ matter), a real number x and L ∈ ℂ, G has radial limit L at x, written HasRadialLimit G x L, if G(x + it/(2π)) → L as t → 0 through positive reals. With q = e^{2πiτ} and G(τ) = g(q) for a function g on the punctured unit disc, this says g(ξe^{−t}) → L as t → 0⁺ with ξ = e^{2πix}: the vertical approach to x is the radial approach to the root of unity ξ from inside the unit disc. The lower version HasRadialLimitBelow G x L means G(x − it/(2π)) → L as t → 0⁺ (functions on the lower half-plane H⁻). The value radialLimit G x is L when a radial limit exists and 0 otherwise. Pinned conventions: q = e^{2πiτ}; the approach parameter is t = 2π·Im τ; x is real (rational x is the case of interest, ξ = e^{2πix} a root of unity). *Hypotheses:* G is arbitrary; no continuity or boundedness hypothesis is part of the definition. Limits are taken in 𝓝[>] 0 for t; the approach is vertical, not non-tangential. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, Theorem 1 and its proof, printed p. 98 and eq. (13), p. 100; Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.3, Definition, printed p. 5.)

Its API is `HasRadialLimit` (HasRadialLimit G x L :⟺ G(x + it/(2π)) → L as t → 0⁺); `HasRadialLimitBelow` (HasRadialLimitBelow G x L :⟺ G(x − it/(2π)) → L as t → 0⁺); `radialLimit` (The radial limit value, L if HasRadialLimit G x L, else 0); `HasRadialLimit.unique` (HasRadialLimit G x L₁ and HasRadialLimit G x L₂ imply L₁ = L₂); `HasRadialLimit.radialLimit_eq` (HasRadialLimit G x L implies radialLimit G x = L); `HasRadialLimit.add` (Radial limits add: HasRadialLimit G x L and HasRadialLimit G' x L' imply HasRadialLimit (G + G') x (L + L')); `HasRadialLimit.const_mul` (HasRadialLimit G x L implies HasRadialLimit (c·G) x (c·L)); `hasRadialLimit_iff_disc` (If G(τ) = g(e^{2πiτ}) on ℍ, then HasRadialLimit G x L ⟺ g(e^{2πix}e^{−t}) → L as t → 0⁺); `HasRadialLimit.of_continuousWithinAt` (If G is continuous at x within the closed upper half-plane {Im ≥ 0}, then HasRadialLimit G x (G x)); `HasRadialLimit.comp_add_one` (If G(τ + 1) = c·G(τ) for all τ ∈ ℍ and HasRadialLimit G x L, then HasRadialLimit G (x + 1) (c·L)).

*Construction.* Define HasRadialLimit G x L as Tendsto (t ↦ G(x + i t/(2π))) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 L), using Mathlib's Filter.Tendsto with the filter nhdsWithin 0 (Ioi 0). Define HasRadialLimitBelow G x L as HasRadialLimit (z ↦ G(z̄)) x L, since conj(x + it/(2π)) = x − it/(2π). Define radialLimit G x by classical choice of L when ∃ L, HasRadialLimit G x L, and 0 otherwise; uniqueness of limits in the Hausdorff space ℂ makes it well defined. Disc form: for G(τ) = g(e^{2πiτ}), e^{2πi(x + it/(2π))} = e^{2πix}e^{−t}, so the definition is the radial limit g(ξe^{−t}) → L; this identification is the API item hasRadialLimit_iff_disc.

*Needs:* Mathlib `UpperHalfPlane`; Mathlib `Complex.exp`.

**Checks.**

- HasRadialLimit (τ ↦ e^{2πiτ}) x (e^{2πix}) for every real x.
- HasRadialLimit (fun _ ↦ c) x c for every c ∈ ℂ and x ∈ ℝ.
- The function τ ↦ e^{2πiτ}/(1 − e^{2πiτ}) has no radial limit at 0.
- HasRadialLimitBelow G x L ⟺ HasRadialLimit (z ↦ G(conj z)) x L.

**Radial asymptotic expansions at rational points.** Define `HasRadialExpansion`. For G : ℂ → ℂ, x ∈ ℝ and a formal power series a = Σ a_r t^r ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, G has radial asymptotic expansion a at x (from above), written HasRadialExpansion G x a, if for every R ∈ ℕ, G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r t^r = O(t^R) as t → 0⁺. From below: HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a :⟺ G(x − it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r (−t)^r = O(t^R) for every R, so that both are expansions in the same variable 2π·Im τ. Following Bringmann–Rolen, functions f on ℍ and g on H⁻ have agreeing asymptotic expansions at x, RadialExpansionsAgree f g x, if some a satisfies HasRadialExpansion f x a and HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a. The series a is not required to converge. *Hypotheses:* The expansion is an asymptotic statement for every order R, in Mathlib's big-O sense along 𝓝[>] 0. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.3, Definition, printed p. 5; Zagier, Mellin, §4, discussion before Proposition 3, printed p. 12.)

Its API is `HasRadialExpansion` (HasRadialExpansion G x a :⟺ ∀ R, G(x + it/2π) − Σ_{r<R} a_r t^r = O(t^R) as t → 0⁺); `HasRadialExpansionBelow` (The lower version, in the same variable 2π·Im τ); `RadialExpansionsAgree` (Bringmann–Rolen agreement of expansions of f on ℍ and g on H⁻ at x); `HasRadialExpansion.unique` (Two radial expansions of G at x are equal); `HasRadialExpansion.hasRadialLimit` (HasRadialExpansion G x a implies HasRadialLimit G x (constantCoeff a)); `HasRadialExpansion.add` (Expansions add); `HasRadialExpansion.mul` (Expansions multiply: HasRadialExpansion (G·G') x (a·a')); `HasRadialExpansion.of_isBigO_all` (If G(x + it/2π) is O(t^R) for every R then HasRadialExpansion G x 0 (flat functions)); `HasRadialExpansion.of_hasSum` (If G(x + it/2π) = Σ_r a_r t^r as a convergent series for 0 < t < ε, then HasRadialExpansion G x a); `RadialExpansionsAgree.radialLimit_eq` (If RadialExpansionsAgree f g x then f and g have the same radial limit at x, from above and below respectively).

*Construction.* Define HasRadialExpansion G x a as ∀ R, (t ↦ G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} coeff r a · t^r) =O[𝓝[>] 0] (t ↦ t^R), with Asymptotics.IsBigO. Define HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a as HasRadialExpansion (z ↦ G(z̄)) x (rescale (−1) a). Define RadialExpansionsAgree f g x as ∃ a, HasRadialExpansion f x a ∧ HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a. Uniqueness: if a and b are both expansions, the difference of the partial sums is O(t^R) for every R, so the coefficients agree inductively (a polynomial of degree < R that is O(t^R) at 0 is zero). The constant term: the case R = 1 gives G(x + it/2π) − a₀ = O(t), hence a radial limit a₀.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Asymptotics.IsBigO`; Mathlib `PowerSeries`; `HasRadialLimit`.

**Checks.**

- HasRadialExpansion (τ ↦ e^{2πimτ}) x (e^{2πimx} • PowerSeries.mk (r ↦ (−m)^r/r!)).
- HasRadialExpansion 0 x 0.
- HasRadialExpansion (τ ↦ e^{−2πi/τ}) 0 0, although the function is not identically zero on ℍ.
- HasRadialExpansion G x a implies HasRadialLimit G x (constantCoeff a).

**The Hurwitz zeta function at s = 0.** Prove `hurwitz_zeta_at_zero`: For x ∈ (0, 1], hurwitzZeta x 0 = 1/2 − x, where x is viewed in ℝ/ℤ (so x = 1 gives hurwitzZeta 0 0 = ζ(0) = −1/2). *Hypotheses:* x ∈ (0, 1]; at x = 0 the formula 1/2 − x is false (the value is ζ(0) = −1/2), which is why the interval is half-open. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, Proposition, eq. (12), printed p. 98; Zagier, Mellin, §4, extension 1, eq. (44), printed p. 13.)

*Proof sketch.* Split hurwitzZeta = hurwitzZetaEven + hurwitzZetaOdd (Mathlib's definition). Even part: hurwitzZetaEven x 0 = −1/2 if x ≡ 0 mod 1 and 0 otherwise (HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaEven_apply_zero). Odd part: the functional equation HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaOdd_one_sub at s = 1 gives hurwitzZetaOdd x 0 = (1/π)·sinZeta x 1. sinZeta x 1 = Σ_{n≥1} sin(2πnx)/n = π(1/2 − x) for 0 < x < 1 (the Fourier series of the sawtooth; its value at the edge s = 1 of the half-plane of absolute convergence is obtained by continuity in s of the analytic continuation and Abel summation of the conditionally convergent series), and sinZeta 0 1 = 0. Add the two parts: for 0 < x < 1 the value is 0 + (1/2 − x); for x = 1 it is −1/2 + 0 = 1/2 − 1.

*Needs:* Mathlib `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta`; Mathlib `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaEven_apply_zero`; Mathlib `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZetaOdd_one_sub`; Mathlib `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat`.

- hurwitzZeta 1 0 = −1/2 = ζ(0).
- The pinned Mathlib proves the formula −B_{k+1}(x)/(k+1) only for k ≠ 0 (HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat); this lemma is the k = 0 case on (0, 1].

**Values of periodic L-functions at non-positive integers.** Prove `periodic_l_value_bernoulli`: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ, with L(s, Φ) = ZMod.LFunction Φ s the meromorphic continuation of Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)n^{−s}. For every integer r ≥ 1, L(−r, Φ) = −(M^r/(r+1)) Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n) B_{r+1}(n/M), with B_k the Bernoulli polynomials. If moreover Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, the same formula holds for r = 0: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} (n/M − 1/2) Φ(n), and L(s, Φ) is entire. *Hypotheses:* M ≥ 1; for r = 0 the mean-zero hypothesis Σ Φ = 0 (otherwise the formula still holds but L has a pole at s = 1 that plays no role; the lemma is stated in the form the sources use). (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, Proposition, eq. (12), printed p. 98; Zagier 2001, §5, formula after the proof of Theorem 6, printed p. 957.)

*Proof sketch.* By definition ZMod.LFunction Φ s = M^{−s} Σ_{j ∈ ZMod M} Φ(j) ζ(j/M, s) with ζ(a, s) the Hurwitz zeta function. For r ≥ 1 insert HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat at x = j.val/M ∈ [0, 1): ζ(x, −r) = −B_{r+1}(x)/(r+1). Reindex j ∈ {0, …, M−1} by n ∈ {1, …, M}, sending j = 0 to n = M; this is allowed because B_{r+1}(1) = B_{r+1}(0) for r + 1 ≠ 1 (bernoulliFun_eval_one). For r = 0 use `hurwitz_zeta_at_zero` with the representatives x = n/M ∈ (0, 1]: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)(n/M − 1/2). Entireness under Σ Φ = 0 is ZMod.differentiable_LFunction_of_sum_zero.

*Needs:* Mathlib `ZMod.LFunction`; Mathlib `ZMod.LFunction_eq_LSeries`; Mathlib `ZMod.differentiable_LFunction_of_sum_zero`; Mathlib `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat`; Mathlib `bernoulliFun_eval_one`; Mathlib `Polynomial.bernoulli`; `hurwitz_zeta_at_zero`.

- For the constant function Φ = 1 on ZMod 1 the r ≥ 1 values are ζ(−r) = −B_{r+1}/(r+1).

**Asymptotics of Σ f((m + a)t) (Euler–Maclaurin).** Prove `euler_maclaurin_asymptotic`: Let f : [0, ∞) → ℂ be C^∞ with every derivative of rapid decay at ∞, let b_n = f^{(n)}(0)/n! and I_f = ∫_0^∞ f(x)dx, and let a ∈ (0, 1]. Then, as t → 0⁺, Σ_{m≥0} f((m + a)t) = I_f/t − Σ_{n<N} b_n (B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1)) t^n + O(t^N) for every N. For a = 1 this is Zagier's Proposition 3: Σ_{m≥1} f(mt) ∼ I_f/t + Σ_n b_n (B_{n+1}/(n+1))(−t)^n. Consequently, for Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ Φ = 0: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n) f(nt) ∼ Σ_n b_n L(−n, Φ) t^n. *Hypotheses:* f smooth on [0, ∞) with f^{(k)}(x) = O(x^{−2}) as x → ∞ for every k (rapid decay suffices). a ∈ (0, 1]. (Zagier, Mellin, §4, Proposition 3, printed p. 12; Zagier, Mellin, §4, extension 1, eq. (44), printed p. 13.)

*Proof sketch.* Apply shifted Euler–Maclaurin on the half-line using the periodised Bernoulli functions with jumps at m+a. Repeated integration by parts, splitting at these lattice points, gives Σ_{m≥0}f((m+a)t)=I_f/t−Σ_{r=1}^{J}B_r(a)f^{(r−1)}(0)t^{r−1}/r! plus a remainder bounded by sup|B̄_J|·t^{J−1}∫₀∞|f^{(J)}|/J!. Use the Bernoulli shift and derivative identities to obtain the boundary coefficients at 0. For the claimed remainder O(t^N), choose J≥N+1, rather than J=N. Rapid decay makes every derivative integrable and kills the boundary terms at infinity. Absorb the retained terms of degree at least N into O(t^N). For a=1 use B_r(1)=(−1)^r B_r(0) to match Zagier Proposition 3. For the periodic corollary split into the M residue classes n=M m+a, a=1,…,M, at scale Mt; the I_f/(Mt) contributions cancel because ΣΦ=0, and `periodic_l_value_bernoulli` identifies the remaining coefficients.

*Needs:* Mathlib `bernoulliFun`; Mathlib `bernoulliFun_eval_one`; Mathlib `Asymptotics.IsBigO`; `periodic_l_value_bernoulli`.

- With a = 1 the lemma reduces to Zagier's Proposition 3 because B_{n+1}(1) = (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}.

**Expansion of Σ Φ(n)e^{−nt} for mean-zero periodic Φ.** Prove `periodic_exponential_sum_asymptotic`: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0. Then Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{r≥0} L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as a convergent power series for 0 < t < 2π/M; in particular the left side has the asymptotic expansion Σ L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as t → 0⁺ and the limit L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M}(n/M − 1/2)Φ(n). *Hypotheses:* Σ Φ = 0 (mean value zero); without it the sum has a pole (ΣΦ/M)/t at t = 0. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, Proposition and its proof, printed pp. 98–99; Zagier 2001, §5, proof of Theorem 6, printed p. 957.)

*Proof sketch.* Sum the geometric series: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)e^{−nt}/(1 − e^{−Mt}). For complex t the quotient t·Σ_{n=1}^M Φ(n)e^{−nt}/(1−e^{−Mt}) has a removable value at 0 and is holomorphic for |t|<2π/M; the denominator has no further zeros there. The mean-zero numerator makes the original quotient removable as well. Compare Taylor coefficients after clearing the denominator with Polynomial.bernoulli_generating_function, which is a formal identity; coefficient recurrence uniqueness identifies them. Analytic Taylor convergence on this disc supplies the asserted HasSum. Do not evaluate a formal series in ℂ merely using PowerSeries.eval₂. The r = −1 term is Σ_n Φ(n)/(Mt), which vanishes by the mean-zero hypothesis. The coefficient of (−t)^r/r! is −M^r/(r+1) Σ_n Φ(n)B_{r+1}(n/M) = L(−r, Φ) by `periodic_l_value_bernoulli`.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.bernoulli_generating_function`; `periodic_l_value_bernoulli`; `HasRadialExpansion`.

**Asymptotic expansion of Σ n^ν Φ(n)e^{−n²t} for mean-zero periodic Φ.** Prove `periodic_gaussian_sum_asymptotic`: Let M ≥ 1, Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, and ν ∈ {0, 1}. As t → 0⁺, Σ_{n≥1} n^ν Φ(n) e^{−n²t} ∼ Σ_{r≥0} L(−2r − ν, Φ)(−t)^r/r!. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, Proposition, printed p. 98; proof, p. 99–100; Zagier 2001, §2, proof of Theorem 3, printed p. 952.)

*Proof sketch.* Apply `euler_maclaurin_asymptotic` to f(x) = x^ν e^{−x²} (smooth, all derivatives of rapid decay) at scale s = √t: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)f(ns) ∼ Σ_n b_n L(−n, Φ) s^n, the I_f/s term cancelling since Σ Φ = 0. For ν = 0 only even n contribute, b_{2r} = (−1)^r/r!, and s^{2r} = t^r. For ν = 1, Σ nΦ(n)e^{−n²t} = s^{−1}Σ Φ(n)f(ns), only odd n = 2r + 1 contribute with b_{2r+1} = (−1)^r/r!, giving Σ L(−2r−1, Φ)(−t)^r/r!.

**The renormalised sum of a mean-zero periodic function.** Prove `renormalised_sum`: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0. ### 5.2 Quantum modular forms and Eichler integrals

**Quantum modular forms (Zagier's canonical definition).** Define `boundaryFactor`. Fix a subgroup Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ), a weight k ∈ ℝ and a multiplier ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ. For γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) and x ∈ ℝ with cx + d ≠ 0, the boundary factor j_k(γ, x) is the limit as y → 0⁺ of the principal power (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k}: it equals |cx + d|^{−k} if cx + d > 0, |cx + d|^{−k}e^{iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c > 0, and |cx + d|^{−k}e^{−iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c ≤ 0 (it is 0 by convention when cx + d = 0). For f : ℚ → ℂ the quantum slash is (f|_{k,ε}γ)(x) = ε(γ)·j_k(γ, x)·f(γx) and the period function is h_γ = f − f|_{k,ε}γ on {x ∈ ℚ : cx + d ≠ 0}. The function f is a quantum modular form of weight k on Γ with multiplier ε if for every γ ∈ Γ there are a finite set S_γ ⊂ ℝ and a function H_γ : ℝ → ℂ, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ S_γ, with H_γ(x) = h_γ(x) for every x ∈ ℚ ∖ S_γ with cx + d ≠ 0. This is Zagier's canonical (weak) definition with P¹(ℝ) replaced by ℝ; the boundary factor is the one of the lower half-plane, which is the branch in which the half-integral weight examples (Eichler integrals of theta series, Kontsevich's function) have constant multipliers. *Hypotheses:* Γ is any subgroup of SL₂(ℤ); in all examples it has finite index. ε is an arbitrary function on SL₂(ℤ); no cocycle condition is imposed in the definition (it enters only through `quantum_modular_cocycle`). Real-analytic means AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H_γ on the open set ℝ ∖ S_γ, for H_γ : ℝ → ℂ. (Zagier QMF, Introduction, printed p. 2; Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §1, after Theorem 1.2, printed pp. 6–7; Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.3, eq. (2.4), printed p. 5.)

Its API is `boundaryFactor` (j_k(γ, x), the lower-half-plane boundary value of (cx + d)^{−k}); `quantumSlash` ((f|_{k,ε}γ)(x) = ε(γ)·j_k(γ, x)·f(γx)); `quantumPeriodFunction` (h_γ = f − f|_{k,ε}γ); `IsQuantumModularForm` (The predicate of the definition); `boundaryFactor_of_pos` (If cx + d > 0 then j_k(γ, x) = (cx + d)^{−k} (real power)); `boundaryFactor_eq_limit` (j_k(γ, x) = lim_{y→0⁺} (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k} with Mathlib's principal Complex.cpow, whenever cx + d ≠ 0); `boundaryFactor_int` (For k ∈ ℤ, j_k(γ, x) = (cx + d)^{−k} (integer power); the branch plays no role in integral weight. For cx+d≠0; no assertion at a pole when k=0); `IsQuantumModularForm.add` (Sums of quantum modular forms of the same (Γ, k, ε) are quantum modular); `IsQuantumModularForm.smul` (Scalar multiples of quantum modular forms are quantum modular); `IsQuantumModularForm.mono` (A quantum modular form on Γ is one on every subgroup Γ′ ≤ Γ); `isQuantumModularForm_of_analyticOnNhd` (For k ∈ ℤ, the restriction to ℚ of a function real-analytic on ℝ is a quantum modular form of weight k on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1); `isQuantumModularForm_iff_generators` (Under ε(1)=1 and the cocycle condition on ε·j_k, it suffices to check the condition on a generating set of Γ (`quantum_modular_cocycle`)).

*Construction.* Define boundaryFactor k γ x by the three cases above; prove it equals lim_{y→0⁺} (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k} for Mathlib's principal cpow (API boundaryFactor_eq_limit). Define quantumSlash k ε γ f x := ε γ * boundaryFactor k γ x * f (γ • x), where γ acts on ℚ by Möbius transformation (0 off the domain). Define quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f := f − quantumSlash k ε γ f. Define IsQuantumModularForm Γ k ε f := ∀ γ ∈ Γ, ∃ S : Finset ℝ, ∃ H : ℝ → ℂ, AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H (↑S)ᶜ ∧ ∀ x : ℚ, (x:ℝ) ∉ S → c x + d ≠ 0 → H x = quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f x. The quantum modular forms of fixed (Γ, k, ε) form a ℂ-subspace: sums and scalar multiples of period functions are period functions, with S the union of the exceptional sets.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`; Mathlib `Complex.cpow`; Mathlib `AnalyticOnNhd`.

**Checks.**

- The constant function 1 on ℚ is a quantum modular form of weight 0 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1 (every period function vanishes).
- The function x ↦ x² on ℚ is a quantum modular form of weight 1 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1.
- The indicator function of ℤ ⊂ ℚ is not a quantum modular form of weight 0 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1.
- For S = (0 −1; 1 0) and x < 0, boundaryFactor (3/2) S x = −i·|x|^{−3/2} (the lower branch), not the principal value i·|x|^{−3/2}.
- For k ∈ ℤ, boundaryFactor k γ x = (γ₁₀x + γ₁₁)^{−k}. Assume cx+d≠0; at a pole the explicit junk convention is 0, including at weight 0.

**The cocycle relation and reduction to generators.** Prove `quantum_modular_cocycle`: Let k ∈ ℝ and ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ, and suppose ε(1)=1 and the factor J(γ, x) := ε(γ)j_k(γ, x) satisfies J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x) for all γ₁, γ₂ ∈ Γ and all x ∈ ℚ outside the finitely many poles involved. Then for f : ℚ → ℂ the period functions satisfy h_{γ₁γ₂} = h_{γ₁}|_{k,ε}γ₂ + h_{γ₂} and h_{γ⁻¹} = −h_γ|_{k,ε}γ⁻¹ (off finitely many points). Consequently, if Γ is generated by a set G and the condition of `boundaryFactor` holds for every γ ∈ G, then f is a quantum modular form on Γ. *Hypotheses:* J satisfies the cocycle condition on Γ (a multiplier system for the lower boundary branch). Normalise ε(1)=1. Together with the cocycle this implies that J(γ,x) and ε(γ) are nonzero on their domains. Without the normalisation the identically zero factor satisfies the printed cocycle but invalidates the inverse relation and generator reduction (take Γ trivial and the empty generating set). (Zagier QMF, Introduction, printed p. 2.)

*Proof sketch.* Expand h_{γ₁γ₂}(x) = f(x) − J(γ₁γ₂, x)f(γ₁γ₂x) and insert J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x): the difference from h_{γ₂}(x) is J(γ₂, x)(f(γ₂x) − J(γ₁, γ₂x)f(γ₁γ₂x)) = (h_{γ₁}|γ₂)(x). The slash of a function real-analytic off a finite set S by γ₂ is real-analytic off γ₂⁻¹(S) ∪ {γ₂⁻¹∞}: Möbius maps and the boundary factor are real-analytic off the pole, where the branch of j_k is locally constant. Apply to γ₁ = γ, γ₂ = γ⁻¹ for inverses (h_1 = 0 when J(1, x) = 1), and induct on word length in G ∪ G⁻¹.

*Needs:* `boundaryFactor`; Mathlib `AnalyticOnNhd`.

**Checks.**

- For k ∈ ℤ and ε a character the cocycle condition is automatic.
- For Kontsevich's function the check reduces to the two generators T and S of SL₂(ℤ) (Zagier, Topology 40, §6).

**Holomorphic Eichler integrals of q-series of real weight.** For integral weight k ≥ 2 this is TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms Layer 8's Eichler integral with coefficients `eichlerCoeff f m = a_m/m^{k−1}`; the definition here allows real weight and polynomially bounded coefficients and agrees with that one at integral weight. Define `eichlerIntegral`. Let w ∈ ℝ, N ≥ 1 and a : ℕ → ℂ with polynomial growth (|a(n)| ≤ Cn^A). For the q-series f(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} a(n)e^{2πinτ/N} (holomorphic on ℍ, no constant term), the Eichler integral of weight w is f̃(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} (n/N)^{1−w} a(n) e^{2πinτ/N} (τ ∈ ℍ), where (n/N)^{1−w} is the positive real power. Writing D = (2πi)^{−1}d/dτ, one has D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1} and f̃_1 = f, so for integer w = k ≥ 1, D^{k−1} f̃ = f: f̃ is the normalised (k − 1)-fold primitive with no constant term. For a cusp form f = Σ a(n)qⁿ of integral weight k on SL₂(ℤ) this is Σ a(n)n^{1−k}qⁿ, the Eichler integral of Tau Ceti's modular symbols layer; for half-integral w it is the formal Eichler integral of Lawrence–Zagier and Bringmann–Rolen. The function f̃ is an analytic object on ℍ; its radial limits and asymptotic expansions at rational points are separate objects (radial-limit, `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1)) and are compared with formal evaluations only by explicit theorems. *Hypotheses:* a has polynomial growth, so the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ. Exponents are n/N ∈ (1/N)ℤ_{>0}; the unary theta series of the sources are the case a supported on squares. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §1, printed p. 1; Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, printed p. 103; Zagier QMF, Example 2, eq. (19), printed p. 8.)

Its API is `eichlerIntegral` (f̃_w(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} (n/N)^{1−w} a(n) e^{2πinτ/N}); `hasSum_eichlerIntegral` (For τ ∈ ℍ the defining series converges absolutely to eichlerIntegral w N a τ); `differentiableOn_eichlerIntegral` (eichlerIntegral w N a is holomorphic on ℍ); `eichlerIntegral_add` (eichlerIntegral is additive in a); `eichlerIntegral_smul` (eichlerIntegral is ℂ-linear in a); `eichlerIntegral_one` (Weight 1: eichlerIntegral 1 N a is the q-series f itself); `deriv_eichlerIntegral` ((2πi)^{−1} d/dτ eichlerIntegral w N a = eichlerIntegral (w − 1) N a on ℍ); `eichlerIntegral_add_N` (eichlerIntegral w N a (τ + N) = eichlerIntegral w N a τ); `eichlerIntegral_unaryTheta` (For a supported on squares, a(n²) = n^ν C(n), weight ν + 1/2: eichlerIntegral = N^{ν−1/2}·Σ n^{1−ν}C(n)q^{n²/N}); `eichlerIntegral_qExpansion` (For f a cusp form of weight k ∈ ℤ on SL₂(ℤ), eichlerIntegral k 1 (qExpansion coefficients of f) = Σ_{n≥1} (coeff n)·n^{1−k}qⁿ, the Tau Ceti modular-symbols Eichler integral); `tendsto_eichlerIntegral_atImInfty` (eichlerIntegral w N a τ → 0 as Im τ → ∞).

*Construction.* Define eichlerIntegral w N a τ := Σ' n ≥ 1, (n/N : ℝ)^(1−w) • a n • exp(2πi n τ/N). Convergence: |(n/N)^{1−w}a(n)e^{2πinτ/N}| ≤ C′n^{A+|1−w|}e^{−2πn Im τ/N}, summable locally uniformly in τ ∈ ℍ; holomorphy by the Weierstrass M-test (Mathlib's locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions). Termwise differentiation: D e^{2πinτ/N} = (n/N)e^{2πinτ/N}, giving D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1}. Unary theta normalisation: for a(m) = n^ν C(n) when m = n² and 0 otherwise (ν ∈ {0,1}), (n²/N)^{1−w} with w = ν + 1/2 equals N^{ν−1/2}n^{1−2ν}, so f̃ = N^{ν−1/2}Σ n^{1−ν}C(n)q^{n²/N}; the sources drop the scalar N^{ν−1/2}.

*Needs:* Mathlib `UpperHalfPlane`; Mathlib `Complex.exp`; Mathlib `ModularForm`; Mathlib `CuspForm`; TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms, Layer 8.

**Checks.**

- eichlerIntegral 1 N a = (τ ↦ Σ a(n)e^{2πinτ/N}).
- Isolating the coefficient a(2)=−24 and setting every other coefficient to zero gives eichlerIntegral 12 1 a(τ)=(−3/256)exp(4πiτ), matching the q² coefficient of Δ̃.
- √24 · eichlerIntegral (1/2) 24 a_η = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}, for a_η(n²) = χ₁₂(n).
- eichlerIntegral w N a τ → 0 as Im τ → ∞, so it differs from any primitive with non-zero constant term.

**The non-holomorphic Eichler integral on the lower half-plane.** Define `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral`. Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ and f = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)qⁿ ∈ S_k(N) a cusp form of half-integral weight on Γ₀(N) (Shimura's multiplier). For τ ∈ H⁻ = {Im τ < 0} define f*(τ) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} f(w)(w − τ)^{k−2} dw, the path running in ℍ from τ̄ to i∞ and (w − τ)^{k−2} the principal branch (w − τ ∈ ℍ). Termwise, f*(τ) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)n^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|Im τ|), with Γ(s, x) = ∫_x^∞ t^{s−1}e^{−t}dt the upper incomplete gamma function. Unlike f̃, f* is real-analytic, not holomorphic, and it has a simple transformation law (`nonholomorphic_eichler_transformation`). *Hypotheses:* f ∈ S_k(N) with k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ (supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7). Γ(k − 1) ≠ 0 for k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ (for k = 1/2, Γ(−1/2) = −2√π). (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.3, printed p. 5; Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, eq. (3.4), printed p. 8; Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, eq. (17), printed p. 103.)

Its API is `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral` (f*(τ) for τ ∈ H⁻, defined by the integral from τ̄ to i∞); `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral_eq_tsum` (f*(τ) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}Σ a_f(n)n^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|Im τ|)); `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral_add` (f ↦ f* is additive); `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral_smul` (f ↦ f* is ℂ-linear); `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral_add_one` (f*(τ + 1) = f*(τ) when f(τ + 1) = f(τ)); `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral_path` (The integral may be taken along any path in ℍ from τ̄ to i∞ that is eventually vertical).

*Construction.* Convergence: f decays exponentially at i∞, and on the vertical path w = τ̄ + iy the factor |(w − τ)^{k−2}| ≤ (2|Im τ| + y)^{k−2}·e^{π|k−2|} is bounded. Path independence in ℍ: the integrand is holomorphic in w on ℍ (w − τ ∈ ℍ never vanishes), so Cauchy's theorem for rectangles moves the path. Termwise integration: ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} e^{2πinw}(w − τ)^{k−2}dw = i^{k−1}(2πn)^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|v|) by the substitution w = τ + iu/(2πn) (BR p. 8), the constants combining because ((−2πi)·i)^{k−1}(2π)^{1−k} = 1 on the principal branches. Real-analyticity requires normal holomorphic extension in independent variables τ and τ̄ near each point of H⁻. On a small complex polydisc avoiding the path and branch cut, the exponentially decaying q-coefficients dominate the incomplete-gamma terms and every derivative. The extended series converges normally there. Locally uniform convergence of real-analytic terms alone would not suffice.

*Needs:* MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7; Mathlib `Complex.Gamma`; Mathlib `Complex.cpow`; Mathlib `Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn`.

**Checks.**

- The non-holomorphic Eichler integral of the zero cusp form is 0.
- For f(w)=exp(2πiw), τ∈H⁻ and k≥1/2, f*(τ)=Γ(k−1)⁻¹exp(2πiτ)Γ(k−1,4π|Im τ|), testing the actual construction and its normalization.
- f* is not the restriction of the holomorphic Eichler integral: for the single exponential, f*(τ) depends on |Im τ| through Γ(k − 1, 4π|Im τ|), so it is not holomorphic in τ.

**The period integral r_α of a half-integral weight cusp form.** Define `eichlerPeriodIntegral`. For f ∈ S_k(N) as in `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral` and a cusp α ∈ ℚ, define r_{f,α}(z) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_α^{i∞} f(w)(w − z)^{k−2}dw for z ∈ H⁻ (principal branch, w − z ∈ ℍ), the path running in ℍ from α to i∞. It extends from H⁻ to a real-analytic function on ℝ ∖ {α} (and holomorphically to ℂ minus any path from α to i∞), and it is the half-integral weight analogue of the period polynomial: in integral weight k ≥ 2 the same integral is a polynomial of degree ≤ k − 2. *Hypotheses:* f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ; α ∈ ℚ. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, after eq. (16), printed p. 103; Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, proof of Theorem 1.1, printed p. 11.)

Its API is `eichlerPeriodIntegral` (r_{f,α}(z), defined on H⁻ by the integral from α to i∞); `analyticOnNhd_eichlerPeriodIntegral` (The boundary restriction x ↦ r_{f,α}(x) is real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {α}); `eichlerPeriodIntegral_sub` (r_{f,α} − r_{f,β} = the integral of f(w)(w − z)^{k−2} from α to β (path in ℍ)); `eichlerPeriodIntegral_add_one` (r_{f,α+1}(z + 1) = r_{f,α}(z) when f is 1-periodic); `eichlerPeriodIntegral_linear` (f ↦ r_{f,α} is ℂ-linear).

*Construction.* Convergence at α: f(w) decays faster than any power of Im(w) as w → α inside a Stolz angle (α is a cusp and f is cuspidal there), and |(w − z)^{k−2}| is bounded near α for z ∉ {α}. Holomorphic continuation: for a path L from α to i∞ in ℍ, the integral defines a holomorphic function of z ∈ ℂ ∖ L (the integrand is holomorphic in z off L); choosing L to leave α vertically and deforming it gives the continuation across ℝ ∖ {α}. Real-analyticity on ℝ ∖ {α} follows by restricting the holomorphic continuation.

*Needs:* `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral`; Mathlib `AnalyticOnNhd`; Mathlib `Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn`.

**Checks.**

- r_{0,α} = 0.
- For k=2 and f(w)=exp(2πiw), the defining integral gives r_{f,α}(z)=exp(2πiα). This computation tests the normalization and orientation; the test function is not asserted to be a cusp form.
- For z ∈ H⁻, r_{f,α}(z) − f*(z) = c_k∫_α^{z̄} f(w)(w − z)^{k−2}dw (path in ℍ), with c_k = (−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1).

**Transformation law of the non-holomorphic Eichler integral (Bringmann–Rolen (2.4)).** Prove `nonholomorphic_eichler_transformation`: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, trivial character), γ = (a b; c d) ∈ Γ₀(N) and τ ∈ H⁻: f*(τ) − χ₋₄(d)·(f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = r_{f,−d/c}(τ), where (g|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d)(cτ + d)^{k−2}g(γτ) is Shimura's slash with the principal branch of (cτ + d)^{k−2} on H⁻, ε_d ∈ {1, i} and χ₋₄ = (−4/·). *Hypotheses:* γ ∈ Γ₀(N); c ≠ 0 (for c = 0 the right side is read as 0 and the statement is the periodicity of f*). (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.3, eq. (2.4), printed p. 5; Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, proof of (ii), printed p. 104.)

*Proof sketch.* Write f*(γτ) as the integral from γτ̄ to i∞ and substitute w = γu: u runs from τ̄ to γ⁻¹(i∞) = −d/c, dw = du/(cu + d)². Use the modularity f(γu) = ε_d^{−2k}(c/d)(cu + d)^k f(u) (Shimura's multiplier, supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7) and w − γτ = (u − τ)/((cu + d)(cτ + d)). Branch bookkeeping: for c > 0, cu + d ∈ ℍ and cτ + d ∈ H⁻, so the arguments add inside (−π, π) and ((cu + d)(cτ + d))^{2−k} splits; arg(u − τ) − arg((cu + d)(cτ + d)) = arg(w − γτ) because both sides lie in (0, π); the case c < 0 is symmetric. This gives (f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{4−4k}·c_k∫_{τ̄}^{−d/c} f(u)(u − τ)^{k−2}du, and ε_d^{4−4k} = ε_d^{−2} = χ₋₄(d) for k ∈ ½ + ℤ. Subtract from f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{i∞}: the difference is c_k∫_{−d/c}^{i∞} = r_{f,−d/c}(τ).

*Needs:* `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral`; `eichlerPeriodIntegral`; MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7; Mathlib `CongruenceSubgroup.Gamma0`; Mathlib `Complex.cpow`.

**Checks.**

- For γ = T = (1 1; 0 1): χ₋₄(1) = 1 and the statement is f*(τ + 1) = f*(τ).
- The right side is independent of τ̄ and extends real-analytically across ℝ ∖ {−d/c}: this is what makes f̃ quantum modular.

**Non-tangential boundary values of f* at cusps.** Prove `nonholomorphic_eichler_nontangential_limit`: For f ∈ S_k(N) as above and x ∈ ℚ, f*(τ) converges as τ → x within any Stolz angle {τ ∈ H⁻ : |Re τ − x| ≤ C|Im τ|}, and the limit equals the radial limit from below of f* at x. *Hypotheses:* f cuspidal at every cusp; k∈½+ℕ₀. This does not imply k−2<0. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, proof of Theorem 1.1, printed pp. 10–11.)

*Proof sketch.* Split f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{x} + c_k∫_{x}^{i∞}, paths in ℍ, the second taken vertically from x. For the vertical ray w=x+iv and τ in a fixed small Stolz neighbourhood, |w−τ|≥v and |w−τ|≤v+C₀. Bound the kernel by e^{π|k−2|}v^{min(k−2,0)}(v+C₀)^{max(k−2,0)}. Cuspidal decay at x and at infinity makes this integrable after multiplication by |f(w)|, for every allowed k. Dominated convergence supplies the boundary limit. Along the segment from τ̄ to x in the Stolz angle, |f(w)|≤C exp(−c/|w−x|). Also |w−τ| is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of |Im τ|. Thus the integral is O(exp(−c′/|Im τ|)|Im τ|^{k−1})→0, for every k. Hence the limit exists within the Stolz angle and equals c_k∫_x^{i∞}f(w)(w − x)^{k−2}dw, which is also the vertical limit.

*Needs:* `nonholomorphicEichlerIntegral`; MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7.

**Checks.**

- The image under γ ∈ Γ₀(N) of the vertical ray below x approaches γx tangentially to the vertical (γ(x − iy) − γx = −iy/(cx + d)² + O(y²)), so it lies eventually in every Stolz angle at γx; this is the use in `half_integral_eichler_quantum_modular` (§5.3).
- The statement fails for tangential approach along a horocycle, which the sources never need.

### 5.3 Mellin transforms and quantum modularity of Eichler integrals

**Twisted L-functions of half-integral weight cusp forms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.2).** Prove `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`: Let f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, and d/c ∈ ℚ in lowest terms. The twisted L-function L_f(ζ_c^d; s) = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)ζ_c^{dn}n^{−s} (Re s ≫ 0, ζ_c^d = e^{2πid/c}) extends to an entire function of s, and L_f(ζ_c^d; −m) = 0 for every m ∈ ℕ₀. *Hypotheses:* f cuspidal; the twisted series converges absolutely for Re s > k/2 + 1 by the Hecke bound a_f(n) = O(n^{k/2}). (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.4, Lemma 2.2, printed p. 6.)

*Proof sketch.* Use the all-cusp holomorphy/decay in the classical half-weight cusp-form input, without decomposing additive twists into nebentypus components. At x=d/c reduced, c>0, choose γ=(d b;c a)∈SL₂(ℤ) and its holomorphic root w_γ(z)=√(cz+a). Put h(z)=w_γ(z)^{−2k}f(γz) and h_x(t)=h(−a/c+it). All-cusp cuspidality gives exponentially decaying Fourier expansions for h_x at ∞ with positive rational frequencies; it gives the same for f(x+iy) at ∞. Since γ^{−1}(x+iy)=−a/c+i/(c²y) and cγ^{−1}(x+iy)+a=i/(cy), the chosen upper-half-plane branch gives the exact identity f(x+iy)=e^{πik/2}(cy)^{−k}h_x(1/(c²y)). This is a scalar identity for the slash by one chosen lift; it needs no assertion that a Fricke involution preserves a particular nebentypus space. Set F_x(s)=∫₀∞f(x+iy)y^{s−1}dy. At both endpoints the preceding exponential estimates, including any fixed power of y and log y, are integrable uniformly for s in compact sets. Hence F_x is entire. Termwise integration initially for Re s>k/2+1 gives F_x(s)=(2π)^{−s}Γ(s)L_f(e(x);s). Therefore L_f(e(x);s)=(2π)^sF_x(s)/Γ(s) is entire and vanishes at every nonpositive integer. The same substitution gives F_x(s)=e^{πik/2}c^{k−2s}H_x(k−s), where H_x(u)=∫₀∞h_x(t)t^{u−1}dt. For c=1 this covers integral x as well; the chosen SL₂ matrix and root keep the central phase explicit. Cusp Fourier frequencies may be rational and have a shift; their Dirichlet sums use those positive frequencies, so no unjustified width-one expansion is introduced.

*Needs:* MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7; Mathlib `mellin`; Mathlib `Complex.Gamma`.

**Checks.**

- The values L_f(ζ; −m) vanish, while the Taylor coefficients of f̃ at d/c are the values at k − 1 − n, which for k ∈ ½ + ℤ are half-integers and in general non-zero.
- The vanishing at non-positive integers is what makes f̃ and f* have the same expansion (the odd powers of √t in f* drop out).

**Exponential decay of Γ on vertical lines (Stirling's estimate).** Prove `gamma_vertical_decay`: For every compact interval [x₁, x₂] ⊂ ℝ there is C such that |Γ(x + iy)| ≤ C|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2} for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and |y| ≥ 1; more precisely |Γ(x + iy)| = √(2π)|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2}(1 + O(1/|y|)) uniformly for x in compact sets. *Hypotheses:* x in a fixed compact interval; |y| ≥ 1 (away from the poles on the real axis). The Stirling asymptotic of log Γ in vertical strips is ZerosOfLFunctions Layer 1 item 3 (a TauCetiRoadmap pull request); this statement is its exponentiated corollary. Brent's explicit remainder bound gives an admissible constant C₀. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, eq. (3.2), printed p. 8; Brent 2016, §2, (5)–(12), Theorem 1, printed pp. 3–5.)

*Proof sketch.* Take ZerosOfLFunctions Layer 1, items 1–3 (TauCetiRoadmap pull request #253; the Gamma estimate that AnalyticNumberTheoryPartI, TauCetiRoadmap pull request #1126, cites for its Layers 1.2–1.4): for every compact [x₁, x₂], log|Γ(x + iy)| = (x − 1/2)log|y| − π|y|/2 + log(2π)/2 + E(x, y) with |E(x, y)| ≤ C₀/|y| for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and |y| ≥ Y₀. The Stirling remainder, the branch of log Γ on |arg s| < π − δ and the uniformity in x are that layer's targets and are not restated here. Exponentiate: for |E| ≤ 1, |e^E − 1| ≤ 2|E|, so |Γ(x + iy)| = √(2π)|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2}(1 + O(1/|y|)) uniformly for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and |y| ≥ max(Y₀, C₀); in particular the normalized modulus lies in [1/2, 3/2] for all large |y|. On the compact set x ∈ [x₁, x₂], 1 ≤ |y| ≤ max(Y₀, C₀), Γ is continuous and nonzero (`Complex.Gamma_ne_zero` away from the nonpositive integers, which have y = 0), so the normalized modulus is bounded above and below there; enlarge the constant. AnalyticNumberTheoryPartII §4.3b (TauCetiRoadmap pull request #1167) states the resulting two-sided bound and balanced quotients from the same input; this statement keeps the stronger relative error, which its uses need.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Complex.Gamma`; Mathlib `Complex.Gamma_ne_zero`; TauCetiRoadmap.ZerosOfLFunctions, Layer 1 (`Complex.norm_Gamma_asymptotic`).

**Checks.**

- |Γ(1/2 + iy)| = √(π/cosh(πy)) ~ √(2π)e^{−π|y|/2}.
- After normalization by sqrt(2π)|y|^(x−1/2)exp(−π|y|/2), the modulus lies between 1/2 and 3/2 for all sufficiently large |y|, uniformly on the fixed strip; this is the lower bound required for gamma quotients.

**Polynomial growth of twisted L-functions in vertical strips (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.3).** Prove `twisted_l_function_vertical_growth`: For f ∈ S_k(N) and d/c ∈ ℚ as in `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`, and every compact interval [x₁, x₂], there are C, A with |L_f(ζ_c^d; x + it)| ≤ C(1 + |t|)^A for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and t ∈ ℝ. *Hypotheses:* As in `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.4, Lemma 2.3, printed p. 7.)

*Proof sketch.* Use the exact cusp identity and entire Mellin integrals constructed in `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`. Write F_x(s)=(2π)^{−s}Γ(s)L_x(s) and H_x(u)=(2π)^{−u}Γ(u)L_h(u), where L_h is the Dirichlet sum of the positive rational-frequency expansion of h_x. Substitution y↦1/(c²y) proves L_x(s)=e^{πik/2}c^{k−2s}(2π)^{2s−k}Γ(k−s)Γ(s)^{−1}L_h(k−s). The powers of the positive real c and 2π and the constant unit phase are fully specified. Far enough right, the coefficient bound O(n^{k/2}) gives uniform absolute bounds for L_x and L_h on vertical lines (a fixed cusp width and frequency shift only change the constant). Far enough left, the displayed identity and the two-sided `gamma_vertical_decay` estimate give a polynomial bound, uniform in Re s in the chosen compact strip. Its positive lower bound for the normalized Γ(s) is used when taking the quotient; the finite t range follows from entire continuation. The Mellin integrals are bounded on any finite vertical strip because |y^{it}|=1 and the endpoint exponential estimates are uniform in Re s. Thus division by Γ(s) gives at most e^{π|t|/2}(1+|t|)^B growth in between. Apply PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip to L_x(s)/(s+B₀)^A, choosing B₀>1−x₁ to avoid a zero denominator on the strip and A large enough for its boundary bounds. This supplies the uniform polynomial estimate throughout. No scalar half-weight Fricke or character decomposition is assumed beyond the all-cusp slash data actually supplied.

*Needs:* `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`; `gamma_vertical_decay`; Mathlib `PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip`.

**Checks.**

- The lemma is exactly what makes Γ(s)L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s) decay rapidly in vertical strips, the hypothesis of `mellin_asymptotic_transfer`.

**Asymptotic expansions from poles of Mellin transforms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.1).** Prove `mellin_asymptotic_transfer`: Let F : (0, ∞) → ℂ be continuous with Mellin transform M(F)(s) = ∫_0^∞ F(x)x^{s−1}dx converging for Re s > α. Suppose M(F) continues meromorphically to a neighbourhood of Re s ≥ β (β < α) with finitely many poles a₀, …, a_M in Re s > β, all simple with residues α₀, …, α_M, is analytic on the line Re s = β, and satisfies M(F)(s) = O(|s|^{−r}) as |Im s| → ∞ in every finite vertical strip β ≤ Re s ≤ c for some r > 1. Then F(x) = Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} + O(x^{−β}) as x → 0⁺. If the hypotheses hold for every β, F has the asymptotic expansion Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} (all orders). *Hypotheses:* F continuous; absolutely convergent Mellin integral on some right half-plane; uniform O(|Im s|^{−r}), r>1, on each finite contour strip β≤Re s≤c, and integrability on the boundary line. No uniform bound as Re s→+∞ is required. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, Lemma 3.1, printed p. 7; Zagier, Mellin, §4, Remark after Proposition 3, printed p. 12.)

*Proof sketch.* Mellin inversion on the line Re s = c > α: F(x) = (2πi)^{−1}∫_{c−i∞}^{c+i∞} M(F)(s)x^{−s}ds (mellinInv_mellin_eq, using the decay for vertical integrability). Move the line to Re s = β: integrate over rectangles [β, c] × [−T, T] (Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn after subtracting the principal parts α_j/(s − a_j)), let T → ∞ using the O(|s|^{−r}) decay on the horizontal sides. The residues contribute α_j x^{−a_j}; the remaining integral on Re s = β is bounded by x^{−β}∫|M(F)(β + it)|dt = O(x^{−β}).

*Needs:* Mathlib `mellin`; Mathlib `mellinInv_mellin_eq`; Mathlib `Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn`; `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1).

- For F(x) = e^{−x}, M(F) = Γ(s) with residues (−1)^n/n! at −n: the lemma recovers e^{−x} = Σ (−x)^n/n! to every order.
- Without the decay hypothesis the conclusion fails: the Mellin transform of a function with an oscillating term like sin(1/x) has the same poles but no such expansion.

**Radial expansion of f̃ at rational points (Bringmann–Rolen (3.1)–(3.3)).** Prove `eichler_integral_asymptotic_expansion`: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ) and d/c ∈ ℚ: f̃(d/c + it/(2π)) ∼ Σ_{n≥0} ((−1)^n/n!)L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1 − n)t^n as t → 0⁺. *Proof sketch.* Termwise Mellin transform: M(t ↦ f̃(d/c + it/2π))(s) = Σ n^{1−k}a_f(n)ζ^{nd}∫_0^∞ e^{−nt}t^{s−1}dt = Γ(s)L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s) for Re s ≫ 0. By `twisted_cusp_form_l_function` the right side is meromorphic on ℂ with possible poles only at s = −n (from Γ), of order at most one, residue (−1)^n/n!·L_f(ζ; k − 1 − n). A zero residue makes the corresponding singularity removable, including every point for f = 0. By `twisted_l_function_vertical_growth` and `gamma_vertical_decay` it decays faster than any power of |s| in every vertical strip. Apply `mellin_asymptotic_transfer` for every β.

*Needs:* `eichlerIntegral` (§5.2); `twisted_cusp_form_l_function`; `twisted_l_function_vertical_growth`; `gamma_vertical_decay`; `mellin_asymptotic_transfer`; `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1).

- For f = η(24τ) this recovers Zagier's expansion of H(ξe^{−t}) in Theorem 6 (after the normalisations of eichler-integral).
- The constant term L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1) is Bringmann–Rolen's Q_f(d/c).

**Poles and residues of the Mellin transform of e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t) (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.2 core).** Prove `incomplete_gamma_mellin_poles`: Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ and G_k(s) = M(t ↦ e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t))(s). For Re s > 0 and Re(k − 1 + s) > 0, G_k(s) = β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s)Γ(k − 1 + s) with β(z; a, b) = ∫_0^z t^{a−1}(1 − t)^{b−1}dt the incomplete beta function; equivalently G_k(s) = 2^{k−1}Γ(s + k − 1)·₂F₁(1, s + k − 1; 1 + s; −1)/s. G_k continues meromorphically to ℂ; its poles lie in −ℕ₀ ∪ {1 − k − m : m ∈ ℕ₀}, are simple, and at s = −n (n ∈ ℕ₀) the residue is Γ(k − 1)/n!. Moreover β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s) is bounded on vertical lines for |Im s| large. Consequently, for an entire function L with L(k − 1 + s) = 0 at the points s = 1 − k − m, Γ(k − 1)^{−1}L(k − 1 + s)G_k(s) has possible poles of order at most one only at s = −n, with residue L(k − 1 − n)/n!. At any such point with zero residue the singularity is removable. *Hypotheses:* k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀; the regularized incomplete beta function I(z; a, b) = β(z; a, b)/B(a, b). The incomplete beta integral at 1/2 initially needs only Re(s)>0; its second parameter is unrestricted there. All boundary hypergeometric displays refer to analytic continuation. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, Lemma 3.2 and its proof, printed pp. 8–10.)

*Proof sketch.* Derive G_k(s)=Γ(s+k−1)β(1/2;s,2−k−s) by absolute Fubini in Re s>0, Re(s+k−1)>0: reverse 0<t<x/2 in ∫t^{s−1}e^t∫_{2t}∞x^{k−2}e^{−x}dx dt and set t=xu. The x-integral is Γ(s+k−1)(1−u)^{−(s+k−1)}. Put v=u/(1−u), giving β(1/2;s,2−k−s)=∫₀¹v^{s−1}(1+v)^{k−2}dv. On a fixed closed strip A≤Re s≤B choose an integer J>−A. Taylor-expand (1+v)^{k−2} through degree J−1 and write the remainder as v^J times a bounded smooth function on [0,1]. The continued integral is the sum of binomial(k−2,j)/(s+j), j<J, and an absolutely convergent holomorphic remainder on Re s>−J. Dominated differentiation on smaller half-planes gives meromorphic continuation; the same bound is uniform on the fixed strip for |Im s|≥1. At s=−n, multiply its residue binomial(k−2,n) by Γ(k−1−n); repeated Gamma recurrence gives Γ(k−1)/n!. The other possible poles come from Γ(s+k−1), at s=1−k−m; these are simple and are cancelled by L(k−1+s)=0. Distinct half-integral k keeps the two sets disjoint. For the hypergeometric comparison, initially Re s>0, use the Euler integral for the analytic function ₂F₁(1,b;1+s;z): s∫₀¹(1−t)^{s−1}(1−zt)^(−b)dt. Its equality with the power series for |z|<1 follows by the binomial series and repeated integration by parts, ∫₀¹t^j(1−t)^{s−1}dt=j!/[s(s+1)⋯(s+j)]. Continue this integral along the negative real segment to z=−1, where no cut is crossed. With b=s+k−1, substitute v=(1−t)/(1+t); the integral becomes s·2^(1−k)β(1/2;s,2−k−s). This gives the displayed factor 2^(k−1)/s directly, without a separate Pfaff theorem. Extend meromorphically in s. The boundary value is analytic continuation, never ordinaryHypergeometric evaluated outside its convergence disc.

*Needs:* Mathlib `mellin`; Mathlib `Complex.Gamma`; Mathlib `Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub`.

- The incomplete gamma and beta functions with complex parameters and the Gauss hypergeometric function at the boundary point −1 are not in the pinned libraries (Tau Ceti's incomplete gamma and beta are for positive real parameters); this statement owns the identities it needs.

**Radial expansion of f* from below (Bringmann–Rolen (3.19)).** Prove `nonholomorphic_eichler_asymptotic_expansion`: For f ∈ S_k(N) and d/c ∈ ℚ: f*(d/c − it/(2π)) ∼ Σ_{n≥0} (1/n!)L_f(ζ_c^d; k − 1 − n)t^n as t → 0⁺. *Hypotheses:* f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §3, eq. (3.19), printed p. 11.)

*Proof sketch.* Termwise Mellin transform of (3.4): M(f*(d/c − it/2π))(s) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}L_f(ζ; k − 1 + s)·M(e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t))(s). Poles and residues: `incomplete_gamma_mellin_poles` together with the vanishing L_f(ζ; −m) = 0 (`twisted_cusp_form_l_function`) at the half-integers s ≤ 1 − k give possible poles of order at most one only at s = −n with residue L_f(ζ; k − 1 − n)/n!. The singularity is removable whenever this residue is zero. Decay in vertical strips: β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s) is bounded for |Im s| large (from (3.9), (3.17) and `gamma_vertical_decay`), and `twisted_l_function_vertical_growth` bounds L; Γ(k − 1 + s) decays exponentially. Apply `mellin_asymptotic_transfer` for every β.

Then f̃ is a quantum modular form of weight 2 − k on Γ₀(N) with multiplier ε(γ) = χ₋₄(d)ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d) for d>0, extended to d<0 by requiring J(−γ,x)=J(γ,x) for J=ε·j_{2−k}; explicitly ε(γ)=ε(−γ)e^{−iπ(2−k)} if c>0 and ε(γ)=ε(−γ)e^{iπ(2−k)} if c≤0, and for every γ ∈ Γ₀(N) its period function extends to the real-analytic function r_{f,−d/c} on ℝ ∖ {−d/c}. *Hypotheses:* f ∈ S_k(N) with trivial character (the character case is treated in `kontsevich_quantum_modular` (§5.4)). Weight 2 − k, multiplier as stated, lower-boundary branch of `boundaryFactor` (§5.2). For negative d, use the stated extension from −γ with positive d; the local positive-denominator Jacobi formula with |d| is not an extended negative-denominator formula. In particular J(−I,x)=1. (Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §1, Theorem 1.1, printed p. 2.)

*Proof sketch.* By `eichler_asymptotic_agreement` the radial limit of f̃ at x equals the radial limit of f* from below at x. Take x ∈ ℚ with cx + d ≠ 0 and let τ = x − iy, y → 0⁺, in `nonholomorphic_eichler_transformation` (§5.2). f*(τ) → f̃(x); (cτ + d)^{k−2} → the boundary factor j_{2−k}(γ, x) of `boundaryFactor` (§5.2) (lower branch); f*(γτ) → f̃(γx) by `nonholomorphic_eichler_nontangential_limit` (§5.2), since γτ approaches γx tangentially to the vertical. The right side r_{f,−d/c}(τ) → r_{f,−d/c}(x), real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {−d/c} (`eichlerPeriodIntegral` (§5.2)). Hence h_γ(x) = r_{f,−d/c}(x) on ℚ ∖ {−d/c}, which is the definition with S_γ = {−d/c}. First prove the law for d>0, as in the native Shimura stand-in. For d<0 apply it to −γ, which acts by the same Möbius transformation, and use the constant ratio of lower boundary factors just stated. This gives the full subgroup law and its trivial central action.

### 5.4 Kontsevich's strange series

**Kontsevich's strange series F(q) = Σ (q;q)_n as an element of the Habiro ring.** The element F = Σ_n (q; q)_n of the Habiro ring is HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §2.1's Kontsevich element, and its values and Taylor expansions are the maps of §§3.1–3.2 there; the definitions here are the finite value function on roots of unity, the Taylor series in t after q = ξe^{−t}, and the normalised function φ on ℚ, each compared with those maps. Define `kontsevichValue`. Kontsevich's series is F(q) = Σ_{n≥0} (q;q)_n with (q;q)_n = (1 − q)(1 − q²)⋯(1 − qⁿ) the finite q-Pochhammer symbol (`qPochhammer` (§0.1)). The series does not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧ nor on any open subset of ℂ, but it converges in the Habiro ring ℤ[q]^ = lim_n ℤ[q]/((q;q)_n) (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§1.4 and 2.1), where the n-th term lies in the n-th ideal; F denotes that element. Its formal evaluations are the images under the Habiro evaluation and Taylor maps (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§3.1–3.2): for a root of unity ξ of order N, F(ξ) = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (ξ;ξ)_n (the terms with n ≥ N vanish), and after the substitution q = ξe^{−t} the Taylor map gives the power series T_ξF = Σ_{n≥0} (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, which converges t-adically because (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ t^{⌊n/N⌋}ℂ⟦t⟧. The normalised function on ℚ is φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}). These are formal evaluations: that they agree with radial limits of a holomorphic q-series is the content of strange-identity, not of this definition. *Hypotheses:* The Habiro ring, its evaluation maps and Taylor maps are HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§1.4 and 2.1 and HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§3.1–3.2. ξ ranges over roots of unity in ℂ; N ≥ 1 with ξ^N = 1 (any such N gives the same finite sum). (Zagier 2001, §2, eq. (15) and following, printed p. 950; Zagier QMF, Example 3, printed pp. 10–11; Zagier 2001, §5, eq. (31), printed p. 956.)

Its API is `kontsevichValue` (F(ξ) = Σ_{n<N}(ξ;ξ)_n for a root of unity ξ with ξ^N = 1 (N chosen as the order)); `kontsevichValue_eq_sum_range` (For every M ≥ 1 with ξ^M = 1, F(ξ) = Σ_{n<M}(ξ;ξ)_n); `kontsevichTaylor` (T_ξF = Σ_n (ξe^{−t};ξe^{−t})_n ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧ (t-adically convergent)); `constantCoeff_kontsevichTaylor` (The constant coefficient of T_ξF is F(ξ)); `kontsevichValue_galois` (For a field automorphism σ of ℂ, σ(F(ξ)) = F(σ(ξ)); in particular F(ξ̄) is the complex conjugate of F(ξ)); `kontsevichPhi` (φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) for x ∈ ℚ); `kontsevichPhi_add_one` (φ(x + 1) = e^{2πi/24}φ(x)); `kontsevichPhi_neg` (φ(−x) is the complex conjugate of φ(x)).

*Construction.* Convergence in the Habiro ring: (q;q)_n ∈ ((q;q)_n), so the partial sums form a compatible system (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§1.4 and 2.1). Evaluation: ev_ξ is continuous and (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ N because the factor 1 − ξ^N vanishes; hence ev_ξ(F) = Σ_{n<N}(ξ;ξ)_n, independent of N with ξ^N = 1. Taylor map: (ξe^{−t};ξe^{−t})_n contains the ⌊n/N⌋ factors 1 − e^{−jNt} (j ≤ n/N), each in tℂ⟦t⟧, so the sum converges in ℂ⟦t⟧ (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.summable_of_tendsto_order_atTop_nhds_top); it is the image of F under the Taylor map at ξ composed with q ↦ ξe^{−t}. Constant coefficient of T_ξF is F(ξ) (the constant term of the Taylor map is evaluation, HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§3.1–3.2). Galois: for σ ∈ Aut(ℂ/ℚ), σ(F(ξ)) = F(σξ) because F(ξ) is a polynomial expression in ξ with integer coefficients.

*Needs:* `qPochhammer` (§0.1); HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§1.4 and 2.1; HabiroCyclotomicCompletions §§3.1–3.2; Mathlib `PowerSeries`; Mathlib `PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.summable_of_tendsto_order_atTop_nhds_top`; Mathlib `IsPrimitiveRoot`.

**Checks.**

- kontsevichValue 1 = 1.
- kontsevichValue (−1) = 3.
- kontsevichValue I = 8 − 3i.
- The coefficients of t⁰, t¹, t² in kontsevichTaylor 1 are 1, 1, 3/2.
- The q-coefficient of Σ_{n≤M}(q;q)_n in ℤ⟦q⟧ is −M, so the partial sums do not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧.

**The sum-of-tails series F₁ = Σ n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ.** Define `sumOfTails`. F₁(q) = Σ_{n≥1} n (q;q)_{n−1} qⁿ ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, which also defines a holomorphic function on the unit disc and, since (q;q)_{n−1} ∈ (1 − q)^{n−1}ℤ[q], a formal power series in 1 − q (and in ξ − q for every root of unity ξ). The companion series is F₂(q) = Σ_{n≥0}[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞] ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, the sum of the tails of Euler's product. The Euler product (q;q)_∞ = ∏_{n≥1}(1 − qⁿ) and E(q) = Σ_{n≥1} qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ) = Σ d(n)qⁿ enter the identity of `zagier_sum_of_tails_identity`. *Hypotheses:* All series are in ℤ⟦q⟧ with the pi topology; convergence as functions on |q| < 1 is absolute and locally uniform. (Zagier 2001, §2, eqs. (17)–(18), printed p. 950.)

Its API is `sumOfTails` (F₁ ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧); `sumOfTailsFun` (F₁ as a holomorphic function on the open unit disc); `tailsSeries` (F₂ = Σ[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞] ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧); `sumOfTails_eq_tailsSeries` (F₁ = F₂ in ℤ⟦q⟧ (partial summation (16) and N → ∞)); `sumOfTailsFun_eq_tsum` (sumOfTailsFun q equals the sum of the power series sumOfTails at q for |q| < 1); `coeff_sumOfTails` (The coefficient of q^m in F₁ is a finite sum over n ≤ m).

*Construction.* F₁ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since the n-th term has order n. F₂ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since (q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞ ∈ q^{n+1}ℤ⟦q⟧. Holomorphy on the disc: |n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ| ≤ n·C(r)|q|ⁿ on |q| ≤ r < 1 with C(r) = ∏(1 + r^j).

*Needs:* `qPochhammer` (§0.1); Mathlib `PowerSeries`; Mathlib `PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.summable_of_tendsto_order_atTop_nhds_top`.

**Checks.**

- The coefficients of q, q², q³ in sumOfTails are 1, 2, 1.
- constantCoeff sumOfTails = 0.
- sumOfTails = tailsSeries in ℤ⟦q⟧.

**F₁ agrees with F to all orders at every root of unity.** Prove `sum_of_tails_agreement`: (a) For every N ≥ 1, Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_N] = Σ_{n=1}^{N} n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ in ℤ[q]. (b) For every root of unity ξ = e^{2πix}, the function τ ↦ F₁(e^{2πiτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion T_ξF (`kontsevichValue`) at x: HasRadialExpansion (F₁ ∘ e^{2πi·}) x (kontsevichTaylor ξ). In particular the radial limit of F₁ at ξ is the formal evaluation F(ξ). *Hypotheses:* ξ a root of unity of order K. (Zagier 2001, §2, eq. (16), printed p. 950; Zagier 2001, §2, proof of Theorem 3, printed p. 952.)

*Proof sketch.* (a) Induction on N (partial summation): passing from N to N + 1 adds (q;q)_N − (N + 1)(q;q)_{N+1} + N(q;q)_N on the left and (N+1)(q;q)_N q^{N+1} on the right, which agree since (q;q)_{N+1} = (q;q)_N(1 − q^{N+1}). From (a): F₁(q) − Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n = Σ_{n>N} n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ − N(q;q)_N for |q| < 1. For q=ξe^{−t}, split the product into K-blocks. Compare block r with ∏_{j=1}^K(1−ξ^j e^{−rKt})=1−e^{−rK²t}. A finite-product telescoping estimate bounds the difference by C_K t e^{−rKt}; hence each block is ≤1+C_K t e^{−rKt}. The product of these bounds is ≤exp(C_K t/(1−e^{−Kt})), uniformly bounded for 0<t≤1. The first m fixed complete blocks each contribute O_m(t), and a last partial block is≤2^K. Therefore |(q;q)_{n−1}|≤C_m t^m uniformly for n>mK. Summing n e^{−nt} gives O(t^{m−2}); choose m as large as needed. The polynomial Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n in q = ξe^{−t} has Taylor expansion agreeing with T_ξF modulo t^m (the omitted terms lie in t^m ℂ⟦t⟧). Letting m grow gives the expansion to every order (HasRadialExpansion), and its constant term gives the radial limit F(ξ).

*Needs:* `sumOfTails`; `kontsevichValue`; `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1); `qPochhammer` (§0.1); `pochhammer_root_of_unity_bound` (§5.7).

**The two-variable identity Σ (x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24}.** Prove `andrews_exercise_identity`: First interpret the sum in (ℤ⟦x⟧)⟦q⟧ with the product topology, where each q-coefficient converges x-adically. Its closed form descends to ℤ[x]⟦q⟧: S(x) := Σ_{n≥0}(x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ_{n≥1} χ₁₂(n) x^{(n−1)/2} q^{(n²−1)/24}, with (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(1 − qx)⋯(1 − qⁿx) and χ₁₂ = (12/·) (only n ≡ ±1 mod 6 contribute, so the exponents are integers). Moreover S(x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ_{n≥0}[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧. *Hypotheses:* The first sum converges coefficientwise x-adically in (ℤ⟦x⟧)⟦q⟧, not q-adically in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧: its summands have nonzero constant q-coefficient (1−x)xⁿ. The recursion proves descent to polynomial q-coefficients; differentiation at x=1 is performed only after this descent. (Zagier 2001, §2, proof of Theorem 2, eq. (23), printed p. 951.)

*Proof sketch.* Form S(a,x)=Σ(a;q)_n xⁿ in the x-adic ring and verify (1−x)S(a,x)=1−axS(a,qx) and S(a,x)=1+(1−a)xS(qa,x) coefficientwise. All rearrangements here are x-adically legitimate. Deduce S(x) = (1 − x)S(qx, x) satisfies S(x) = 1 − qx² − q²x³S(qx). The right side R(x) = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24} satisfies the same equation: −q²x³R(qx) reindexed by m = n + 6 gives Σ_{m≥7}χ₁₂(m)x^{(m−1)/2}q^{(m²−1)/24}, using χ₁₂(n + 6) = −χ₁₂(n) and (m² − 1)/24 = (n² − 1)/24 + (n + 3)/2. Uniqueness: the map T ↦ 1 − qx² − q²x³T(qx) raises q-order, so it has a unique fixed point in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧; hence S = R, and in particular each q-coefficient of S is a polynomial (in fact a monomial) in x. The second expression: split (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(qx;q)_n and write Σ(qx;q)_n xⁿ(1 − x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ; each q-coefficient involves only n < q-degree.

- A consequence (Zagier's Remark): Σ nχ(n)q^{n²/24}/Σ χ(n)q^{n²/24} = 1 − 2Σ qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ)·(1 + 1/((1 − q)⋯(1 − qⁿ))).

**Euler's product vanishes to infinite order at every root of unity.** Prove `eta_infinite_order_vanishing`: For every rational x, the function τ ↦ (q;q)_∞ = ∏(1 − e^{2πinτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion 0 at x; more precisely, for x = a/c in lowest terms (c ≥ 1), |(q;q)_∞| ≤ C·y^{−1/2}exp(−π/(12c²y)) for q = e^{2πi(x+iy)}, 0 < y ≤ 1. The same holds for E(q)·(q;q)_∞, since |E(q)| ≤ Σ n|q|ⁿ = O(y^{−2}). *Hypotheses:* x ∈ ℚ; the constant C depends on x. (Zagier 2001, §2, proof of Theorem 3, printed p. 952; Bringmann–Rolen 2015a, §2.2, printed p. 5.)

*Proof sketch.* Choose γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with γ(∞) = a/c and write τ = x + iy = γτ′; then Im τ′ = 1/(c²y). The transformation law η(γτ′) = ψ(γ)(cτ′ + d)^{1/2}η(τ′) (`etaMultiplier` (§1.2)) gives |η(τ)| = |cτ′ + d|^{1/2}|η(τ′)| with |cτ′ + d| = 1/(cy). |η(τ′)| ≤ C′e^{−2π Im τ′/24} for Im τ′ ≥ 1, and (q;q)_∞ = e^{−2πiτ/24}η(τ). Every power y^m dominates exp(−π/(12c²y)), so the expansion is 0 to all orders; multiply by the O(y^{−2}) bound for E.

*Needs:* `etaMultiplier` (§1.2); Mathlib `ModularForm.eta`; Mathlib `ModularForm.eta_comp_eq_csqrt_I_inv`; `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1).

**Checks.**

- At x=0 and t>0, |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_∞| = √(2π/t)e^{−π²/(6t)}e^{t/24}(e^{−4π²/t};e^{−4π²/t})_∞. In particular it is bounded above by the same expression with the last product omitted, and their ratio tends to 1.
- Because the expansion is 0, the mean of m ↦ χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} over a period vanishes (otherwise `euler_maclaurin_asymptotic` (§5.1) would give a term of order t^{−1/2}); this is used in `kontsevich_value_formula`.

**Kontsevich–Zagier strange identity at every root of unity.** Prove `strange_identity`: Let ξ = e^{2πix} (x ∈ ℚ) and H(q) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}. The holomorphic function τ ↦ H(e^{2πiτ}) on ℍ has radial asymptotic expansion −2·T_ξF at x, where T_ξF = kontsevichTaylor ξ is the formal Taylor expansion of the Habiro element F at ξ in the variable t (q = ξe^{−t}). In particular its radial limit at ξ is −2F(ξ); equivalently, with η̃(τ) = Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}, the radial limit of η̃ at x is −2φ(x). This is the exact meaning of the ‘strange identity’ Σ (q;q)_n “=” −½Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}: a comparison between a formal evaluation (left) and the radial limits and asymptotic expansions of a q-series convergent only in the disc (right). *Hypotheses:* ξ an arbitrary root of unity (all orders, including even and non-prime-power orders). (Zagier 2001, Introduction, after eq. (7), printed p. 947; Zagier QMF, Example 3, printed p. 10.)

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 2 (`zagier_sum_of_tails_identity`) holds as an identity of holomorphic functions on the disc: −½H = F₁ − (½ − E)(q;q)_∞. F₁ has radial expansion T_ξF at x (`sum_of_tails_agreement`). (q;q)_∞ and E(q)(q;q)_∞ have radial expansion 0 at x (`eta_infinite_order_vanishing`). Add the expansions (HasRadialExpansion.add); multiply by −2.

*Needs:* `zagier_sum_of_tails_identity`; `sum_of_tails_agreement`; `eta_infinite_order_vanishing`; `kontsevichValue`; `HasRadialExpansion` (§5.1); `HasRadialLimit` (§5.1).

- At ξ = 1: e^{−t/24}F(e^{−t}) = Σ T_n(t/24)ⁿ/n! with the Glaisher numbers T_n = 1, 23, 1681, … (Zagier's Theorem 3; see `kontsevich_value_formula`).
- At ξ = −1 the radial limit of H is −2F(−1) = −6.
- The identity is not an identity of power series in q: F has no q-expansion, and H has no values on the unit circle; only their expansions at roots of unity are compared.

**Values and Taylor coefficients of F at roots of unity as twisted L-values.** Prove `kontsevich_value_formula`: Let ξ = e^{2πiα} and N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1, and let Φ_ξ(m) = χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} (a function on ZMod N, with ξ^{s} := e^{2πiαs}). Define c_n(ξ) by e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!) (the Taylor expansion of `kontsevichValue`). Then c_n(ξ) = (−1)^{n−1}L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)/2 = (−1)ⁿN^{2n+1}/(2n + 2)·Σ_{m=1}^{N/2}Φ_ξ(m)B_{2n+2}(m/N); in particular F(ξ) = (1/(4N))Σ_{m=1}^{N} m²Φ_ξ(m), and at ξ = 1 the c_n(1) are the Glaisher numbers T_n given by Σ T_n x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! = sin 2x/(2 cos 3x). *Hypotheses:* N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1 (so Φ_ξ is N-periodic). (Zagier 2001, §5, Theorem 6, printed p. 956; Zagier 2001, §5, after the proof of Theorem 6, printed p. 957; Zagier 2001, §2, Theorem 3, printed p. 952.)

*Proof sketch.* Φ_ξ is N-periodic: ((m + N)² − m²)/24 = (N/12)(2m + N)/2 with (2m + N)/2 ∈ ℤ for odd m. Φ_ξ has mean zero: Σ_{m≥1}Φ_ξ(m)e^{−m²t/24} = e^{−t/24}(q;q)_∞ at q = ξe^{−t}, which tends to 0 (`eta_infinite_order_vanishing`), while a non-zero mean would contribute a term of order t^{−1/2} by `euler_maclaurin_asymptotic` (§5.1). By `periodic_gaussian_sum_asymptotic` (§5.1) (ν = 1) applied to Φ_ξ at t/24: e^{−t/24}H(ξe^{−t}) ∼ Σ L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)(−t/24)ⁿ/n!. By strange-identity this equals −2e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = −2Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!); compare coefficients. Evaluate L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ) by `periodic_l_value_bernoulli` (§5.1) and fold the sum using Φ_ξ(N − m) = Φ_ξ(m) and B_{2n+2}(1 − x) = B_{2n+2}(x). For n = 0 expand B₂(x) = x² − x + 1/6 and use Σ Φ_ξ = 0 and Σ mΦ_ξ(m) = 0 (from the symmetry m ↔ N − m). At ξ = 1 (N = 12): Σ_m χ₁₂(m)e^{−mt} = sinh 2t/cosh 3t (partial fractions over one period), whose coefficients give the stated generating function by `periodic_exponential_sum_asymptotic` (§5.1).

*Needs:* `strange_identity`; `periodic_gaussian_sum_asymptotic` (§5.1); `periodic_exponential_sum_asymptotic` (§5.1); `periodic_l_value_bernoulli` (§5.1); `euler_maclaurin_asymptotic` (§5.1); `eta_infinite_order_vanishing`; Mathlib `ZMod.LFunction`.

- F(1) = (1/48)(1 − 25 − 49 + 121) = 1.
- c₁(1) = T₁ = 23 and c₂(1) = 1681.
- F(−1) = 3 and F(i) = 8 − 3i from the formula with N = 24 and N = 48 respectively (agreeing with `kontsevichValue`).

**Kontsevich's function is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2.** Prove `kontsevich_quantum_modular`: The function φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) on ℚ satisfies φ(x + 1) = e^{2πi/24}φ(x) and φ(x) + (ix)^{−3/2}φ(−1/x) = g(x) (x ∈ ℚ, x ≠ 0), where (ix)^{−3/2} is the principal branch and g : ℝ → ℂ is C^∞, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {0}, with g^{(n)}(0) = (−πi/12)ⁿc_n (c_n the Glaisher numbers). Equivalently, φ is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2 on SL₂(ℤ) (`boundaryFactor` (§5.2), lower boundary branch) with multiplier ε determined by ε(T) = e^{−2πi/24} and ε(S) = e^{2πi/8}, ε(γ)=v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c≠0 or d>0, and ε(γ)=−v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c=0,d<0; hence ε(−I)=−i and ε(−I)j_{3/2}(−I,x)=1. For general γ the period function is real-analytic except at γ⁻¹∞. *Hypotheses:* Use the lower-boundary multiplier ε(γ)=v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c≠0 or d>0, and ε(γ)=−v_η(γ)⁻¹ for c=0,d<0. Its values at T and S are the stated inverse eta values, but its value at −I differs from the naive inverse. The corrected factor satisfies QuantumCocycleCondition and acts trivially at −I. (Zagier 2001, §6, Theorem, printed pp. 958–959; Zagier QMF, Example 3, printed p. 10.)

*Proof sketch.* φ(x) = −½·(radial limit of η̃ at x) by strange-identity, η̃ = √24·(Eichler integral of weight 1/2 of η) (eichler-integral). Put D_gamma(z)=cz+d and v_gamma=v_eta(gamma). On the upper half-plane the eta transformation law and eta nonvanishing show that A_gamma(z)=v_gamma^(-1) D_gamma(z)^(-1/2) is a multiplicative automorphy factor. Squaring the eta law, using (D_gamma(z)^(1/2))^2=D_gamma(z) and the ordinary denominator cocycle, shows that gamma maps to v_gamma^2 is a character. For w in the lower half-plane, conjugate A_gamma(conj(w)). Since |v_gamma|=1, this is s_gamma v_gamma D_gamma(w)^(-1/2), where s_gamma=-1 exactly when c=0,d<0, and s_gamma=1 otherwise: only the negative-real principal-power cut prevents conjugation from commuting with the half power. Multiply this conjugated factor by the character v_gamma^(-2) and the integral-weight factor D_gamma(w)^(-1). The product is s_gamma v_gamma^(-1) D_gamma(w)^(-3/2), hence satisfies the full factor cocycle. Take lower boundary limits away from intermediate and product poles to obtain QuantumCocycleCondition for epsilon=s_gamma v_gamma^(-1). In particular epsilon(-I)=-i and epsilon(-I)j_(3/2)(-I,x)=1. This establishes consistency of the factor, not the analytic transformation of the Kontsevich function. For the analytic transformation use the actual lower Eichler integral Eη(z)=C∫_{z̄}^{i∞}η(w)(w−z)^{−3/2}dw with C=(−2πi)^{−1/2}/Γ(−1/2). The negative Gamma argument causes no endpoint singularity because w−z stays in ℍ. For T, translate the integration variable and use η(w+1)=e(1/24)η(w); for S use η(−1/w)=√(−iw)η(w), dw↦w^{−2}dw and S(w)−S(z)=(w−z)/(wz). On w=it,z=−iy (t,y>0), the transformed kernel divided by the original is −y^{3/2}; this fixes its constant branch on the connected domain. Multiplication by ε(S)j_{3/2}(S,z)=−y^{−3/2} gives Eη−ε(S)jEη∘S equal to its period integral from 0 to i∞. For T the period is zero. The already proved factor cocycle extends these identities to words in S,T; the transformed paths concatenate to the period from γ⁻¹∞. The central element acts by 1, as checked above. The rational-boundary comparison does not require a scalar nebentypus comparison. In η=Σ_{n≥1}χ₁₂(n)e(n²τ/24), at x∈ℚ the coefficients Φ_x(n)=χ₁₂(n)e(xn²/24) are periodic and even. Their mean is zero: the Gaussian Poisson constant term equals that mean, while the eta S/T transformation and its zero constant term give exponential decay at x. Thus its periodic L-function is entire; the even-parity negative-integer zeros cancel the unwanted half-integer Mellin poles. The termwise incomplete-Gamma integral, finite Taylor subtraction and Mellin contour displacement from nodes361–364 apply to this explicit L-function, with frequency n²/24 and the scalar √24 dictated by eichler-integral. They give agreement of every coefficient, not only the constant boundary value. The lower integral has the required nontangential limit because eta decays exponentially after a cusp scaling matrix at every rational endpoint. On a short cusp segment, any fixed power of its height is dominated by that decay; on the remaining path the kernels converge uniformly and an integrable majorant applies. These estimates also apply to γz as z approaches a rational point. Pass to lower boundary values in the exact analytic law, then use strange-identity and the −1/2 normalization relating φ to the eta Eichler series. Prove smoothness of the period integral at 0 by differentiating its boundary kernel to every order under the integral: η(w) decays faster than any power as w→0 on the vertical path and exponentially at infinity, furnishing the derivative majorants. Evaluate these integrals by Mellin continuation and `kontsevich_value_formula` to get g^{(n)}(0)=(−πi/12)ⁿc_n. An asymptotic expansion along the sequence ±1/k alone does not prove smoothness.

*Needs:* `strange_identity`; `eichlerIntegral` (§5.2); `nonholomorphic_eichler_transformation` (§5.2); `eichlerPeriodIntegral` (§5.2); `eichler_asymptotic_agreement` (§5.3); `nonholomorphic_eichler_nontangential_limit` (§5.2); `boundaryFactor` (§5.2); `quantum_modular_cocycle` (§5.2); `kontsevich_value_formula`; `etaMultiplier` (§1.2); Mathlib `ZMod.LFunction`; `eta_transformation_law` (§1.2); Mathlib `ModularForm.eta_ne_zero`; Mathlib `UpperHalfPlane.denom_cocycle`.

- The factor (ix)^{−3/2} equals e^{−3πi/4}x^{−3/2} for x > 0 and e^{3πi/4}|x|^{−3/2} for x < 0; relative to the lower boundary factor of `boundaryFactor` (§5.2) this is the constant −ε(S) = −e^{2πi/8}, which is why the lower branch is pinned.
- Consistency check with Kontsevich's asymptotics: φ(1/k) = e^{2πi(3−k)/24}k^{3/2} + Σ c_n(−πi/(12k))ⁿ/n! + o(1) as k → ∞.
- At gamma = -I the lower-boundary factor of weight 3/2 is i. The corrected multiplier epsilon(-I) = -i gives total slash factor 1. Using the unmodified inverse eta multiplier i would instead give -1, so it fails this central-element check.

**Cohen's terminating evaluations of σ and σ* at roots of unity.** Define `cohenSigma`. For a root of unity ξ define σ(ξ) = 1 + Σ_{n≥0}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and σ*(ξ) = −2Σ_{n≥0}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n (Andrews' and Cohen's expressions (8) evaluated at q = ξ). Both sums terminate: (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord ξ and (ξ²;ξ²)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord(ξ²). These are formal evaluations of Ramanujan's σ(q) = Σ q^{n(n+1)/2}/((1+q)⋯(1+qⁿ)) and its partner σ*(q) = 2Σ(−1)ⁿq^{n²}/((1−q)⋯(1−q^{2n−1})); the latter converge only for |q| < 1, and the agreement of their q-expansions with (8) (Andrews' identity) is not part of this definition. *Hypotheses:* ξ a root of unity; the finite sums are taken up to any bound past the terminating index. (Zagier QMF, Example 1, eq. (8) and following, printed p. 5.)

Its API is `cohenSigma` (σ(ξ) by the terminating sum (8)); `cohenSigmaStar` (σ*(ξ) by the terminating sum (8)); `cohenSigma_eq_sum_range` (For every M≥1 with ξ^M = 1, σ(ξ) = 1 + Σ_{n<M}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n); `cohenSigmaStar_eq_sum_range` (For every M≥1 with (ξ²)^M = 1, σ*(ξ) = −2Σ_{n<M}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n); `cohenSigma_galois` (σ(σ₀(ξ)) = σ₀(σ(ξ)) for field automorphisms σ₀ of ℂ, and likewise for σ*); `cohenSigma_one` (σ(1) = 2).

*Construction.* Define cohenSigma ξ := 1 + Σ_{n<N}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and cohenSigmaStar ξ := −2Σ_{n<N}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n with N = orderOf ξ. Independence of the cut-off: the terms with n ≥ N vanish because they contain the factor 1 − ξ^N (resp. 1 − ξ^{2j} with ord(ξ) | 2j ≤ 2n).

*Needs:* `qPochhammer` (§0.1); Mathlib `IsPrimitiveRoot`.

**Checks.**

- cohenSigma 1 = 2.
- cohenSigma I = −2i − 4.
- cohenSigmaStar 1 = −2.

**Cohen's telescoping identity (9).** Prove `cohen_telescoping_identity`: Let S_k = Σ_{n=1}^{k} q^{−n(n−1)/2}(1 + q)(1 + q²)⋯(1 + q^{k−n}) ∈ ℤ[q, q⁻¹]. Then for every k ≥ 0, in ℤ[q, q⁻¹]: Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}(q⁻¹ − 1)⋯(q^{−n} − 1) − Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}q^{n+1}(1 − q²)⋯(1 − q^{2n}) = (1 − q)⋯(1 − q^k)·S_k. *Hypotheses:* k ≥ 0; the identity is in the Laurent polynomial ring. (Zagier QMF, Example 1, proof of the Lemma, eq. (9), printed p. 5.)

*Proof sketch.* The recursion S_{k+1} − S_k = q^{k+1}(S_{k+1} − (1 + q)⋯(1 + q^k)) − q^{−k(k+1)/2}, by comparing the two sums term by term. Induction on k: the case k = 0 is 0 = 0; the step multiplies the recursion by (1 − q)⋯(1 − q^k) and uses (1 − q^{j})(1 + q^{j}) = 1 − q^{2j}.

*Needs:* Mathlib `LaurentPolynomial`.

**Checks.**

- k = 1: 1 − q = (1 − q)·S₁ with S₁ = 1.
- k = 2: 1 + (q⁻¹ − 1) − q − q²(1 − q²) = (1 − q)(1 − q²)(1 + q + q⁻¹).

**Cohen's duality σ(q) = −σ*(q⁻¹) at roots of unity.** Prove `cohen_sigma_duality`: For every root of unity ξ, cohenSigma ξ = −cohenSigmaStar ξ⁻¹. *Hypotheses:* ξ a root of unity. (Zagier QMF, Example 1, Lemma, printed p. 5.)

*Proof sketch.* Evaluate `cohen_telescoping_identity` at q = ξ with k ≥ ord ξ: the right side vanishes because (1 − ξ)⋯(1 − ξ^k) contains the factor 1 − ξ^{ord ξ} = 0. The first sum on the left equals ½σ(ξ⁻¹): with P_n = (ξ^{−1} − 1)⋯(ξ^{−n} − 1) one has ξ^{−n−1}P_n = P_{n+1} + P_n, so ½ + ½Σ_{n<k}ξ^{−n−1}P_n = Σ_{n<k}P_n + ½P_k and P_k = 0; and σ(ξ⁻¹) = 1 + Σ ξ^{−n−1}P_n since (−1)ⁿ(1 − ξ^{−1})⋯(1 − ξ^{−n}) = P_n. The second sum is −½σ*(ξ) by definition. Hence σ(ξ⁻¹) + σ*(ξ) = 0; replace ξ by ξ⁻¹.

*Needs:* `cohen_telescoping_identity`; `cohenSigma`.

**Checks.**

- ξ = −1: σ(−1) = −2 = −σ*(−1).
- ξ = ω: σ(ω) = −σ*(ω²) = 2ω + 6.
- The statement is about formal evaluations only; the quantum modularity of x ↦ e^{2πix/24}σ(e^{2πix}) (Zagier's Proposition) needs Cohen's Maass form and is not decomposed here.

### 5.5 The Poincaré homology sphere

**The periodic functions χ₊ and χ₋ of period 60.** Define `lzChiPlus`. χ₊, χ₋ : ℤ → {−1, 0, 1} are the functions of period 60 given by χ₊(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 1 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise, and χ₋(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 49 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise (n taken in [0, 60)). They are the real and imaginary parts of the primitive character χ = (12/·)ε of conductor 60, where ε is the character of conductor 5 with ε(1, 2, 3, 4) = (1, −i, i, −1). As functions on ZMod 60, χ₊ takes the value 1 at 1, 11, 19, 29 and −1 at 31, 41, 49, 59. *Hypotheses:* n is reduced to [0, 60) before ⌊n/30⌋ is taken; equivalently χ₊ is odd and 60-periodic. (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, printed p. 102; Zagier QMF, Example 4, printed pp. 11–12.)

Its API is `lzChiPlus` (χ₊ : ZMod 60 → ℤ); `lzChiMinus` (χ₋ : ZMod 60 → ℤ); `lzChiPlus_ne_zero_iff` (χ₊(n) ≠ 0 ⟺ n² ≡ 1 (mod 120)); `lzChiPlus_neg` (χ₊(−n) = −χ₊(n), and likewise for χ₋); `sum_lzChiPlus` (Σ_{n mod 60} χ₊(n) = 0 (mean zero), and likewise for χ₋); `lzChiPlus_eq_re` (χ₊ = Re((12/·)ε) and χ₋ = Im((12/·)ε) as functions on ZMod 60).

*Construction.* Define lzChiPlus, lzChiMinus : ZMod 60 → ℤ by the table, and prove the congruence descriptions by deciding the finitely many cases. The identification with Re and Im of (12/·)ε is a finite check over ZMod 60. Oddness χ±(−n) = −χ±(n) and mean zero Σ_{n mod 60} χ±(n) = 0 are finite checks.

*Needs:* Mathlib `ZMod.LFunction`.

**Checks.**

- lzChiPlus 11 = 1 and lzChiPlus 49 = −1 and lzChiPlus 7 = 0.
- For every n, lzChiPlus n = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if gcd(n, 6) = 1 and n ≡ ±1 (mod 5), and 0 otherwise.
- Σ_{n : ZMod 60} lzChiPlus n = 0.
- lzChiPlus is not multiplicative: lzChiPlus 7 = 0 but lzChiPlus 49 = −1.

**The Eichler-integral series A(q) of the Poincaré sphere.** Define `lzSeries`. A(q) = Σ_{n≥1} χ₊(n)q^{(n²−1)/120} ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧ (the exponents are integers because n² ≡ 1 mod 120 when χ₊(n) ≠ 0); it converges on |q| < 1 and A(q) = 1 + q + q³ + q⁷ − q⁸ − q¹⁴ − q²⁰ − ⋯ . With q = e^{2πiτ}, Θ̃₊(τ) := q^{1/120}A(q) = Σ_{n≥1}χ₊(n)q^{n²/120} is the Eichler integral of the weight-3/2 theta series Θ₊(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₊(n)q^{n²/120} in Lawrence–Zagier's normalisation, and √120·Θ̃₊ = eichlerIntegral (3/2) 120 applied to the coefficients of Θ₊. Θ̃₋ is defined in the same way with χ₋. *Hypotheses:* q^{1/120} = e^{2πiτ/120} on ℍ (no branch choice). (Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §3, eq. (11), printed p. 98; Lawrence–Zagier 1999, §4, printed p. 103.)

Its API is `lzSeries` (A(q) ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧); `lzSeriesFun` (A as a holomorphic function on the unit disc); `lzThetaTilde` (Θ̃±(τ) = Σ χ±(n)q^{n²/120} on ℍ); `lzThetaTilde_eq` (Θ̃₊(τ) = e^{2πiτ/120}·lzSeriesFun(e^{2πiτ})); `lzThetaTilde_eq_eichlerIntegral` (√120·Θ̃₊ = eichlerIntegral (3/2) 120 a with a(n²) = nχ₊(n)); `coeff_lzSeries` (The coefficient of q^m in A is χ₊(n) if 120m + 1 = n², and 0 otherwise).

*Construction.* Define lzSeries := PowerSeries.mk (m ↦ Σ_{n : n² = 120m + 1} χ₊(n)) — at most one n contributes. Define lzThetaTilde± τ := Σ_{n≥1}χ±(n)e^{2πin²τ/120}. Compare with eichler-integral: for a(n²) = nχ₊(n), weight 3/2 and N = 120 the normalisation factor is N^{1/2}.

*Needs:* `lzChiPlus`; `eichlerIntegral` (§5.2); Mathlib `PowerSeries`.

**Checks.**

- The coefficients of q⁰, q¹, q², q³, q⁸ in lzSeries are 1, 1, 0, 1, −1.
- constantCoeff lzSeries = 1.
- Every coefficient of lzSeries lies in {−1, 0, 1}.

**WRT invariants of the Poincaré sphere as radial limits (Lawrence–Zagier Theorem 1).** Prove `lawrence_zagier_radial_limit`: Let W(ξ) = ξ(ξ − 1)Z(ξ), where Z(ξ) is the sl₂ Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of the Poincaré homology sphere Σ(2, 3, 5) at the root of unity ξ (ArithmeticQuantumTopology §4.2, normalised by Z(S³) = 1; W(1) = 0). Then for every root of unity ξ the radial limit of 1 − ½A(q) as q → ξ exists and equals W(ξ).
