### 5.6 Cranks, ranks and Ramanujan's congruences

**The Andrews–Garvan crank of a partition.** Define `partitionCrank`. For a partition λ of n (Mathlib's Nat.Partition n), let ℓ(λ) be its largest part (0 for the empty partition), ω(λ) the number of parts equal to 1, and μ(λ) the number of parts larger than ω(λ) (counted with multiplicity). The crank is c(λ) = ℓ(λ) if ω(λ) = 0 and c(λ) = μ(λ) − ω(λ) if ω(λ) > 0; it is an integer with |c(λ)| ≤ n. *Hypotheses:* λ ranges over Nat.Partition n; the empty partition of 0 has crank 0. (Andrews–Garvan 1988, §1, Definition, printed p. 168; Andrews–Garvan 1988, §3, table, printed p. 170.)

Its API is `partitionCrank` (c(λ) ∈ ℤ); `partitionCrank_of_numOnes_eq_zero` (If λ has no parts equal to 1 then c(λ) = ℓ(λ)); `partitionCrank_of_numOnes_pos` (If λ has a part equal to 1 then c(λ) = μ(λ) − ω(λ)); `partitionCrank_indiscrete` (For n ≥ 2 the one-part partition (n) has crank n); `partitionCrank_ones` (For n ≥ 1 the partition 1ⁿ has crank −n); `abs_partitionCrank_le` (|c(λ)| ≤ n for λ ⊢ n).

*Construction.* Define largestPart λ := λ.parts.sup (0 if empty), numOnes λ := λ.parts.count 1, numPartsAbove λ := (λ.parts.filter (· > numOnes λ)).card. Define partitionCrank λ := if numOnes λ = 0 then (largestPart λ : ℤ) else numPartsAbove λ − numOnes λ. The bound |c(λ)| ≤ n: ℓ(λ) ≤ n, and μ, ω ≤ number of parts ≤ n.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Nat.Partition`.

**Checks.**

- The multiset of cranks of the partitions of 6 is {6, 0, 4, −1, 3, 1, −3, 2, −2, −4, −6}.
- The crank of the unique partition of 1 is −1.
- The partition 5 + 1 of 6 has crank 0 but rank 3 (dyson-rank), so the crank is not the rank.
- The cranks of the eleven partitions of 6 are pairwise incongruent modulo 11.

**The crank counts M(m, n) and M(k, t, n).** Define `crankCount`. For m ∈ ℤ and n ∈ ℕ, M(m, n) is the number of partitions of n with crank m when n ≠ 1, and at n = 1 the convention M(0, 1) = −1, M(±1, 1) = 1, M(m, 1) = 0 otherwise (the vector-partition count N_V(m, 1) of Garvan, which makes the generating function exact). For t ≥ 1 and k ∈ ZMod t, M(k, t, n) = Σ_{m ≡ k (mod t)} M(m, n) (a finite sum since M(m, n) = 0 for |m| > n). *Hypotheses:* n = 1 is the only exceptional value; for n > 1, M(m, n) is a genuine count (Andrews–Garvan Theorem 1). (Garvan 1988, §5, Announcement, printed p. 44; Garvan 1988, §5, Theorem 8, printed p. 44.)

Its API is `crankCount` (M(m, n) with the n = 1 convention); `crankCountMod` (M(k, t, n) for k ∈ ZMod t); `sum_crankCount` (Σ_m M(m, n) = p(n) = card (Nat.Partition n)); `sum_crankCountMod` (Σ_{k ∈ ZMod t} M(k, t, n) = p(n)); `crankCount_neg` (M(−m, n) = M(m, n) (from the symmetry z ↔ z⁻¹ of `crank_generating_function`)); `crankCount_eq_zero_of_lt` (M(m, n) = 0 if |m| > n); `crankCount_one` (M(0, 1) = −1, M(±1, 1) = 1).

*Construction.* Define crankCount m n := if n = 1 then (if m = 1 ∨ m = −1 then 1 else if m = 0 then −1 else 0) else #{λ : Nat.Partition n | partitionCrank λ = m}. Define crankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ∈ [−n, n], (m : ZMod t) = k} crankCount m n. Σ_m M(m, n) = p(n): for n ≠ 1 every partition has exactly one crank; for n = 1, −1 + 1 + 1 = 1 = p(1).

*Needs:* `partitionCrank`; Mathlib `Nat.Partition`.

**Checks.**

- Σ_m crankCount m 6 = 11.
- crankCountMod 11 k 6 = 1 for every k : ZMod 11.
- crankCount 0 1 = −1 and crankCount 1 1 = 1 and crankCount (−1) 1 = 1.
- crankCount 0 1 = −1, whereas the number of partitions of 1 with crank 0 is 0.

**The crank generating function (Andrews–Garvan).** Prove `crank_generating_function`: In the ring of formal power series in q with coefficients Laurent polynomials in z (LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, pi topology): Σ_{n≥0} (Σ_m M(m, n)z^m) qⁿ = ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿ)/((1 − zqⁿ)(1 − z⁻¹qⁿ)), each factor being invertible (constant coefficient 1). *Hypotheses:* Formal identity; the infinite product converges q-adically. (Andrews–Garvan 1988, §2, proof of Theorem 1, eq. (2.3), printed p. 169; Andrews–Garvan 1988, §1, eq. (1.11) and Theorem 1, printed pp. 168–169.)

*Proof sketch.* Rewrite the product as (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ · (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞. Cauchy's q-binomial theorem Σ_j (a;q)_j t^j/(q;q)_j = (at;q)_∞/(t;q)_∞ (formal, from Layer 0) with a = zq, t = q/z gives (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞ = Σ_j (zq;q)_j (q/z)^j/(q;q)_j, hence the product is (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ + Σ_{j≥1} q^j z^{−j}/((q²;q)_{j−1}(zq^{j+1};q)_∞). For j ≥ 1 the j-th term generates the partitions with exactly j ones, the exponent of z being μ(λ) − ω(λ) = c(λ): the ones give q^j z^{−j}, 1/(q²;q)_{j−1} the parts 2, …, j, and 1/(zq^{j+1};q)_∞ the parts > j, each counted by z. The j = 0 term (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ generates, for n ≥ 2, the partitions without ones weighted by z^{ℓ(λ)} (conjugation: 1/(zq;q)_∞ counts all partitions by largest part, q/(zq;q)_∞ those with a 1, except at n = 1 where adding a 1 changes the largest part). At n = 1 the coefficient is (z − 1) + z⁻¹, which is the convention of crank-count.

*Needs:* `crankCount`; `qPochhammer` (§0.1); Mathlib `LaurentPolynomial`; Mathlib `PowerSeries`; Mathlib `Nat.Partition.genFun`; Mathlib `HasProd`.

- Setting z = 1 gives Σ p(n)qⁿ = 1/(q;q)_∞ (Nat.Partition.genFun).

**Equidistribution from a vanishing sum over a prime-order root of unity.** Prove `equal_classes_from_root_of_unity`: Let t be a prime, ζ ∈ ℂ a primitive t-th root of unity and c : ZMod t → ℚ. If Σ_{k ∈ ZMod t} c(k)ζ^k = 0 then c is constant; hence if Σ_k c(k) = P then c(k) = P/t for every k. *Hypotheses:* t prime (for composite t the conclusion fails: 1 + ζ² = 0 for t = 4). (Garvan 1988, §4, proof of Theorem 3, printed pp. 38–39.)

*Proof sketch.* The minimal polynomial of ζ over ℚ is the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_t (Polynomial.cyclotomic_eq_minpoly_rat), which for t prime is 1 + X + ⋯ + X^{t−1} (Polynomial.cyclotomic_prime). P(X) = Σ_{k=0}^{t−1} c(k)X^k has degree ≤ t − 1 and P(ζ) = 0, so Φ_t ∣ P and P = c·Φ_t for a constant c.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.cyclotomic_eq_minpoly_rat`; Mathlib `Polynomial.cyclotomic_prime`; Mathlib `IsPrimitiveRoot`; Mathlib `IsPrimitiveRoot.geom_sum_eq_zero`.

- For t = 4, c = (1, 0, 1, 0) gives Σ c(k)i^k = 0 but c is not constant: primality is needed.

**The crank explains p(5n + 4) ≡ 0 (mod 5).** Prove `crank_mod_five`: For every n ≥ 0 and k ∈ ZMod 5, M(k, 5, 5n + 4) = p(5n + 4)/5. *Hypotheses:* n ≥ 0. (Garvan 1988, §4, after Theorem 3, eq. (4.23), printed p. 39; Garvan 1988, §5, Corollary (5.9), printed p. 44.)

*Proof sketch.* Substitute z = ζ = e^{2πi/5} in `crank_generating_function`: Σ_k M(k, 5, N)ζ^k is the coefficient of q^N in C(ζ; q) = (q;q)_∞/((ζq;q)_∞(ζ⁻¹q;q)_∞). From ∏_{k=0}^{4}(1 − ζ^k x) = 1 − x⁵: (q;q)_∞(ζq;q)_∞⋯(ζ⁴q;q)_∞ = (q⁵;q⁵)_∞, so C(ζ; q) = (q;q)_∞·[(ζ²;q)_∞(ζ⁻²q;q)_∞(q;q)_∞]/((q⁵;q⁵)_∞(1 − ζ²)). Jacobi's triple product (TauCetiRoadmap.ClassicalArithmeticCompletion §4.40) gives (ζ²;q)_∞(ζ⁻²q;q)_∞(q;q)_∞ = Σ_m (−1)^m ζ^{2m}q^{m(m−1)/2}, and Euler's pentagonal theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow) gives (q;q)_∞ = Σ_n (−1)ⁿq^{n(3n−1)/2}. Mod 5, m(m−1)/2 takes the values 0, 0, 1, 3, 1 and n(3n−1)/2 the values 0, 1, 0, 2, 2 (m, n ≡ 0, …, 4); the sum is ≡ 4 only for m ≡ 3, n ≡ 1, where ζ^{2m} = ζ is constant. The involution m ↦ 1 − m preserves m ≡ 3 (mod 5) and m(m − 1)/2 and changes (−1)^m, so the q^{5N+4}-part of the product vanishes; dividing by the q⁵-series (q⁵;q⁵)_∞ preserves this. Hence Σ_k M(k, 5, 5n + 4)ζ^k = 0; apply `equal_classes_from_root_of_unity` with Σ_k M(k, 5, 5n + 4) = p(5n + 4) (sum_crankCountMod).

**The crank explains p(11n + 6) ≡ 0 (mod 11).** Prove `crank_mod_eleven`: For every n ≥ 0 and k ∈ ZMod 11, M(k, 11, 11n + 6) = p(11n + 6)/11. *Hypotheses:* n ≥ 0. Its constant nonzero factor relative to η(τ)²/E_{0,1}(τ) is 1−ζ. Jacobi triple product and the stated eta/theta transformation laws give F*|₁A=F* for A∈Γ₀(p²)∩Γ₁(p). Explicitly the remaining phase is exp(πi((d−1)/p+cd/p²−c/p)); its numerator p(d−1)+cd−cp is divisible by p² and even. This proves triviality, rather than assuming a generic eta quotient has trivial character. Project with U_p: S(τ)=p^{−1}Σ_{r=0}^{p−1}F*((τ+r)/p). For A=(a b;c d)∈Γ₁(p), T_r=(1 r;0 p) gives T_rA=B_rT_{r′}, r′≡b+r mod p and B_r=(a+rc,(b+rd−r′(a+rc))/p;pc,d−r′c)∈Γ₀(p²)∩Γ₁(p). Thus S is a weight 1 form on Γ₁(p), holomorphic in ℍ. Root filtering gives S=∏_{j≥1}(1−q^{pj})Σ_{n≥1}(Σ_m M(m,p,pn−5)ζ^m)q^n. The exceptional crank coefficient at n=1 cannot enter the residue6 class. Compute cusp bounds by applying the same two rank-two matrix factorizations according as a+rc is zero or nonzero mod p. The transformed E factors have orders ℓ/(2p)−ℓ²/(2p²), 1≤ℓ<p, and the eta ratio has order determined by Σ_{d|p²}gcd(c,d)²r_d/(24d). These are explicit nonvanishing product expansions, so no cancellation can lower the minimum order. Sarma Theorem 4.5 gives, at p=11: order≥0 at 0 and 1/m (2≤m≤5), and invariant order≥5/11 at m/11 (2≤m≤5). Cusp widths are 11 for 0,1/m, and 1 for ∞,m/11. Holomorphic weight 1 local expansions have integral orders at width 1 cusps, so the last four each contribute at least1. At ∞, S starts in degree 1; enumerating the eleven partitions of 6 gives one in every crank class, so that coefficient is 0 and ord∞S≥2. All interior orders are nonnegative. Hence a nonzero S would have total divisor degree at least2+4=6. The projective index of Γ₁(11) is 60, and the weight 1 valence degree is 60/12=5. This contradiction proves S=0. Cancel the unit ∏(1−q^{11j}); for every n≥0 the residue6 crank polynomial vanishes at ζ. The minimal polynomial 1+X+⋯+X¹⁰ forces all eleven integer coefficients equal; summing gives p(11n+6)/11.

**Dyson's rank and the rank counts N(m, n).** Define `dysonRank`. The rank of a partition λ is ℓ(λ) − #parts(λ) (largest part minus number of parts; 0 for the empty partition). N(m, n) is the number of partitions of n with rank m (so N(0, 0) = 1, the convention of Folsom–Ono–Rhoades (1.4); Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer and Garvan set N(0, 0) = 0), and N(k, t, n) = Σ_{m ≡ k (mod t)} N(m, n). *Hypotheses:* The two conventions for N(0, 0) differ only in the constant term of the generating function. (Garvan 1988, §2, printed p. 31; Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §1, eq. (1.4), printed p. 5.)

Its API is `dysonRank` (rank(λ) = ℓ(λ) − #parts(λ)); `dysonRankCount` (N(m, n)); `dysonRankCountMod` (N(k, t, n)); `dysonRank_conjugate` (There is an involution λ ↦ λ′ of the partitions of n (conjugation, TauCeti.conjugate) with rank(λ′) = −rank(λ)); `dysonRankCount_neg` (N(−m, n) = N(m, n)); `sum_dysonRankCount` (Σ_m N(m, n) = p(n)).

*Construction.* Define dysonRank λ := (largestPart λ : ℤ) − card λ.parts, dysonRankCount m n := #{λ ⊢ n | dysonRank λ = m}, dysonRankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ≡ k} dysonRankCount m n. Conjugation (Tau Ceti's TauCeti.conjugate, an involution by TauCeti.conjugate_conjugate) exchanges largest part and number of parts, so rank(λ′) = −rank(λ) and N(−m, n) = N(m, n).

*Needs:* Mathlib `Nat.Partition`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.conjugate`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.conjugate_conjugate`.

- The rank of the partition 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 of 16 is −3.
- dysonRankCountMod 5 k 4 = 1 for every k : ZMod 5.
- The rank of the empty partition of 0 is 0 and dysonRankCount 0 0 = 1.
- dysonRankCountMod 11 1 6 = 2, so the rank does not divide the partitions of 6 into eleven equal classes.

**The rank generating function R(z; q) (Durfee square).** Prove `rank_generating_function`: In LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧: Σ_{n≥0}Σ_m N(m, n)z^m qⁿ = 1 + Σ_{n≥1} q^{n²}/((zq;q)_n(z⁻¹q;q)_n) =: R(z; q). In particular R(−1; q) = Σ_{n≥0} q^{n²}/(−q;q)_n² is Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function f(q), whose coefficient of qⁿ is N(0, 2, n) − N(1, 2, n). *Hypotheses:* Formal identity; the series converges q-adically since the n-th term has order n². (Garvan 1988, §4, proof of Theorem 4, eq. (4.28), printed p. 40; Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §1, Remark (2) after Theorem 1.2, printed p. 6.)

*Proof sketch.* Decompose a non-empty partition by its Durfee square, the largest n × n square in its Young diagram: the square contributes q^{n²}. The part to the right of the square is a partition with at most n parts; by conjugation its generating function with z marking its largest part is 1/(zq;q)_n. The part below the square is a partition with parts ≤ n; with z⁻¹ marking its number of parts its generating function is 1/(z⁻¹q;q)_n. The rank is (n + largest part of the right piece) − (n + number of parts of the lower piece), matching the exponent of z; the empty partition gives the constant 1.

*Needs:* `dysonRank`; `qPochhammer` (§0.1); Mathlib `LaurentPolynomial`; Mathlib `PowerSeries`.

- R(−1; q) = 1 + q − 2q² + 3q³ − 3q⁴ + 3q⁵ − 5q⁶ + ⋯ (the coefficients of f(q)).

(Garvan 1988, §2, printed p. 31; Garvan 1988, §4, Theorem 4, printed p. 40; Garvan 2016, Theorem 5.1, Proposition 6.2(i), Theorems 6.3(i),6.9,6.11 and §6.3, preprint pp. 25–45.)

Its nonholomorphic terms cancel by finite unary-theta orthogonality; the resulting weakly holomorphic weight 1 function is invariant under Γ₀(p²)∩Γ₁(p), as in Theorem 5.1. The only correction terms that could survive U_p have p-translation character e(3(p−1)ℓ²/(2p)), with 0<ℓ<p; this is nontrivial. Their p translates sum to 0. Thus Proposition 6.2(i), at m=0, gives K_{p,0}=∏_{j≥1}(1−q^{pj})Σ_{n≥1}(Σ_rN(r,p,pn−s_p)ζ_p^r)q^n, with no residual mock correction. The same explicit T_rA=B_rT_{r′} factorization displayed in `crank_mod_eleven` proves Γ₁(p) modularity of the filtered function, now using the J_p transformation. This is the actual content of Theorem 6.3(i), not an inference from an uncompleted rank generating series being modular. For cusp bounds, factor T_rA with a+rc≠0 mod p through Γ₀(p), and with a+rc=0 through (p 0;0 1) followed by S. ### 5.7 Radial limits of the rank and crank functions

**Uniform bounds for q-Pochhammer symbols near roots of unity.** Prove `pochhammer_root_of_unity_bound`: Let ξ = e^{2πih/k} with gcd(h, k) = 1 and let w ∈ ℂ with w^k = 1 and w ∈ ⟨ξ⟩. For q = ξe^{−t} (0 < t ≤ 1): (i) |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_k for all n; (ii) for every m ≥ 1 there is C_{k,m} with |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_{k,m}t^m for all n ≥ (m + 1)k. The constants do not depend on n or t. *Hypotheses:* w a root of unity lying in the cyclic group generated by ξ (for w = 1 this covers (q;q)_n itself). (Zagier 2001, §2, proof of Theorem 3, printed p. 952; Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §3.2, printed p. 19.)

*Proof sketch.* Group the factors 1 − wq^j into blocks of k consecutive indices j = rk + 1, …, rk + k; with x_r = e^{−rkt} a block equals ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x_r e^{−it}). Unperturbed, ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x) = 1 − w^kx^k = 1 − x^k because {wξ^i} is the full group of k-th roots of unity; the perturbation e^{−it} changes the block by at most C′_k x_r t. Hence |block_r| ≤ min(1, (r + 1)k²t) + C′_k x_r t; the product over r ≥ m of (1 + C′_k x_r t) is at most exp(C′_k t Σ_r e^{−rkt}) ≤ exp(C′_k(1+1/k)) since t/(1−e^{−kt})≤t+1/k≤1+1/k, bounded. The first m blocks give O(t^m); the last incomplete block is bounded by 2^k. Combine.

*Needs:* `qPochhammer` (§0.1).

**Checks.**

- For w = 1 and ξ = 1: |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_n| ≤ n!tⁿ from 1 − e^{−jt} ≤ jt.
- Termwise bounds by ∏(1 + |q|^j) are useless here (they grow like e^{c/t}); the block cancellation is essential.

**The unimodal-sequence series U(w; q) and its values at roots of unity.** Define `unimodalSeries`. U(w; q) = Σ_{n≥0}(wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1} ∈ LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, the generating function Σ u(m, n)(−w)^m qⁿ of strongly unimodal sequences of size n and rank m. For a root of unity w = ζ_b^a and ζ = ζ_k^h with b | k, gcd(a, b) = gcd(h, k) = 1, the formal value U(w; ζ) = Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}(wζ;ζ)_n(w⁻¹ζ;ζ)_nζ^{n+1} is a finite sum (the terms with n ≥ k vanish, since some factor 1 − wζ^j is 0). This formal value is distinct from the radial limit of U(w; q) as q → ζ; they are equal by `pochhammer_root_of_unity_bound`, which is a theorem and not part of the definition. *Hypotheses:* b | k for the formal value; for b ∤ k the series does not terminate (e.g. U(−1; e^{2πi/3}), where no factor 1 + ζ^j vanishes). (Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §1, eq. (1.6), printed p. 5; Folsom–Ono–Rhoades 2013, §1, Remark (1) after Theorem 1.2, printed p. 6.)

Its API is `unimodalSeries` (U(w; q) with w a Laurent-polynomial variable); `unimodalValue` (The terminating value U(ζ_b^a; ζ_k^h) for b | k); `unimodalValue_eq_sum_range` (For k>0, b|k and gcd(h,k)=1, every M≥k gives the same terminating value. Primitivity of ζ_k^h is essential); `sum_pochhammer_eq_unimodalSeries` (Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(w;q)_n(w⁻¹;q)_n = (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q)); `unimodalValue_neg_one` (For ζ of order 2k′, U(−1; ζ) = Σ_{n<k′}(−ζ;ζ)_n²ζ^{n+1}).

*Construction.* Define unimodalSeries w as Σ_n (wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1}, convergent q-adically (the n-th term has order n + 1). Define unimodalValue a b h k := Σ_{n<k}(ζ_b^aζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_n(ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_nζ_k^{h(n+1)}. Termination: since b | k, ζ_b^a = ζ_k^{ha′} for some a′, so 1 − ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^{hj} = 0 for j ≡ a′ (mod k), which occurs among j ≤ k. Relation: Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(w;q)_n(w⁻¹;q)_n = (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q), from (w;q)_{n} = (1 − w)(wq;q)_{n−1}.

*Needs:* `qPochhammer` (§0.1); Mathlib `LaurentPolynomial`; Mathlib `PowerSeries`; Mathlib `IsPrimitiveRoot`.

In particular the n=−r terms are exactly q^r(α⁻¹;q)_r(β⁻¹;q)_r, not a divergent continuation of a unilateral series. Its proof takes the two numerator parameters a,c of Bailey’s ₂ψ₂ transformation (2.4) to infinity after z↦zq/(ac), b=βq,d=αq, and finally z=αβ. This supplies a proof of the generic identity, rather than only its αβ=1 specialization. The bilateral seed is obtained by Chen–Fu Proposition 3.1 (3.3): shift the lower endpoint −m to 0, use (x;q)_{n−m}=(x;q)_{−m}(xq^{−m};q)_n, apply their unilateral transformation(3.2), then let m→∞. It follows by equating coefficients in Heine’s q-Euler transformation; Heine’s transformation itself follows by expanding one product ratio with Cauchy’s q-binomial theorem, interchanging the double sum, and summing the other variable by the same theorem (Gasper(3.4.2)–(3.5.1)). Insert this convolution into the right-hand ₃φ₂ in Chen–Fu(3.2) and set n=k+j. Its inner sum is ₂φ₁(aq^k,y;axyq^k;q,x)=(xyq^k,axq^k)_∞/(axyq^k,x)_∞, by q-Gauss, obtained from the same Heine transformation at its Gauss argument. Multiplication by the prefactor P=(x,axy)_∞/(ax,xy)_∞ leaves (axy)_k/((ax)_k(xy)_k); cancellation gives exactly the left-hand ₃φ₂(a,b,c;d,ax;q,xy). Initially choose |x|,|xy|<1 and pole-free parameters in a compact subdomain where the double sums converge absolutely. Chen–Fu’s four strict bounds in(3.1) similarly give geometric bounds on both bilateral tails, permitting m→∞. Meromorphic continuation and the same tail bounds justify the numerator-parameter limits in Mc Laughlin. This ends the seed in the existing q-binomial and convergence inputs, rather than a book-only hypergeometric identity. Substitute the existing definition μ(u,v;z)=α^{1/2}ϑ(v;z)^{−1}Σ_r(−1)^rβ^r q^{r(r+1)/2}/(1−αq^r). The triple product is ϑ(v;z)=−iq^{1/8}β^{−1/2}(β;q)_∞(q/β;q)_∞(q;q)_∞. Cancel (β⁻¹;q)_∞=(1−β⁻¹)(q/β;q)_∞ and (β;q)_∞=(1−β)(βq;q)_∞. The constants give precisely the displayed iq^{1/8}(1−α)exp(πi(v−u)) factor. For α=w⁻¹,β=w the negative part is (1−w)(1−w⁻¹)U(w;q), proving the required rank specialization.

For δ_l=l−(k−1)/2, partition ν∈ℤ+1/2 uniquely as ν=kμ+δ_l, μ∈ℤ+1/2, 0≤l<k. Since |δ_l|<k/2, sgnν=sgnμ; the error-function argument becomes that for T=k²τ and V=kv+kδ_lτ+(k−1)/2. Completing squares and tracking the parity gives R(v;τ)=Σ_l(−1)^l i^{k−1}exp(−πiδ_l²τ−2πiδ_lv)R(V;k²τ). This is Bringmann–Folsom Proposition 2.3 with τ replaced by kτ. At v=−2a/b, τ=(h+iz)/k, the real part of V is −2ak/b+lh−(k−1)(h−1)/2∈ℤ, by b|k and coprimality. Crucially its final R and Mordell arguments are τ₀=i/(kz), the S-transform of ikz; they are not ikz. Thus Z′=h′/k+τ₀ and both R series below have the same imaginary part. For Σ₂+Σ₃ use theta transformation and elliptic translation to obtain FOR(3.19), retaining the eighth-root multiplier ρ(γ). Divide by the common nonzero theta factor and write τ=Z′, y=Im τ, τ₀=τ−h′/k. For real c the series is explicitly R(c;τ₀)=Σ_{ν∈ℤ+1/2} sgn(ν)Γ(1/2,2πν²y)/√π ·(−1)^{ν−1/2} exp(−πiν²τ)exp(πiν²h′/k−2πiνc); R(2ah′/b;τ) has the same formula with the last factor replaced by exp(−4πiνah′/b). Therefore the difference of FOR(3.20) and(3.21) is a normally convergent sum of pure nonholomorphic Fourier terms Γ(1/2,4πny)q′^{−n}, n=ν²/2>0, with coefficients obtained by the finite l-sum with weights exp(−πihδ_l²/k)e(2al/b)(−1)^{l(h+1)}. The Mordell integral is holomorphic in τ₀ by Gaussian domination on compact subsets. Applying ∂/∂barτ to the pure Γ expansion and Fourier uniqueness on a common rational period forces each coefficient, after pairing ν and −ν, to vanish. There is neither a ν=0 term nor a holomorphic Fourier part in this displayed expansion. Consequently the difference is 0, establishing the exact cancellation without an unsupported zero-shadow inference or an extra transformed-R Fourier theorem. For Σ₁ use the defining Appell sum at Z′ and u=ah′/b: its n=0 term is e^{πiu}/(1−e(u)); the positive and negative n tails are O(q₁), after replacing denominators in the negative tail by their reciprocal form. Hence exp(−2πc_lx)/cosh(πx) is bounded and every Gaussian moment is integrable; after x=√(kz)t its integral is O(√z). For U, choose N≥(m+1)k. The terms n≥N have both Pochhammer factors O(t^m) uniformly by `pochhammer_root_of_unity_bound`, so their sum is O(t^{2m−1}). The finitely many terms k≤n<N tend to 0 since they contain a factor vanishing at the limiting root. The terms n<k tend to the terminating value. A tail beginning at the fixed index k is not uniformly O(t^m) for arbitrary m.

### 5.8 Traces of singular moduli

**Positive definite forms of discriminant −d, their CM points and weights.** The forms are Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.BinaryQuadraticForm ℤ` with its SL(2, ℤ) action; Q_d is `TauCeti.BinaryQuadraticForm.posDef d`, the reduced representatives are `TauCeti.reducedForms d`, and H(d) is `TauCeti.hurwitzClassNumber d`. The new objects are the CM point and the stabiliser order. Define `heegnerForms`. For an integer d > 0 with d ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 4), Q_d is the set of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms Q = [a, b, c] = aX² + bXY + cY² (a > 0) with b² − 4ac = −d, primitive or not, with the action of Γ = PSL₂(ℤ) by (Q∘γ)(X, Y) = Q(aX + bY, cX + dY). Its CM point is the unique root α_Q = (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ of Q(X, 1), and w_Q = |Γ_Q| is the order of its stabiliser in PSL₂(ℤ): w_Q = 2 if Q ∼ [a, 0, a], 3 if Q ∼ [a, a, a], 1 otherwise. Q_d/Γ is finite (every class contains a unique reduced form |b| ≤ a ≤ c, with b ≥ 0 if |b| = a or a = c), and the weighted count Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}1/w_Q is the Hurwitz–Kronecker class number H(d). *Hypotheses:* d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4); for d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4), Q_d is empty. H(d) is Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.hurwitzClassNumber d`, the weighted count of reduced forms with weights 1/2 and 1/3. (Zagier, Traces, §1, printed p. 1–2.)

Its API is `heegnerForms` (Q_d, the positive definite forms of discriminant −d); `cmPoint` (α_Q ∈ ℍ); `stabiliserOrder` (w_Q = |Γ_Q| ∈ {1, 2, 3}); `heegnerClasses` (A finite set of reduced representatives of Q_d/Γ); `cmPoint_smul` (α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹·α_Q); `stabiliserOrder_eq` (w_Q = 2 iff Q ∼ [a, 0, a], w_Q = 3 iff Q ∼ [a, a, a], and w_Q = 1 otherwise); `sum_inv_stabiliserOrder` (Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}1/w_Q = H(d), the Hurwitz class number of Tau Ceti's modular forms layer 11); `heegnerForms_eq_empty` (Q_d = ∅ if d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4)).

*Construction.* Define heegnerForms d as {Q : Fin 3 → ℤ | Q 0 > 0 ∧ Q 1² − 4·Q 0·Q 2 = −d} with the right action of SL₂(ℤ) through its image in PSL₂(ℤ). cmPoint Q := (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ; it satisfies α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹α_Q (Möbius action), so it depends only on the orbit up to the action. Take the reduced-form representatives and reduction theory from TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms layer11 rather than replanning it. Add the CM-point/action comparison to that existing representation; reduction gives a≤√(d/3) and the finite orbit representatives. stabiliserOrder Q := card of the stabiliser of Q in PSL₂(ℤ), equal to the stabiliser of α_Q, which is trivial except at the orbits of i and ρ = e^{2πi/3}.

*Needs:* Mathlib `UpperHalfPlane`; Mathlib `Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`; Mathlib `ModularGroup.S`; Mathlib `ModularGroup.T`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.hurwitzClassNumber`.

- The weighted count Σ 1/w_Q over heegnerClasses 12 is 4/3.
- heegnerForms 5 = ∅.

**The modular trace t(d) of the singular moduli of discriminant −d.** Define `modularTrace`. With J(τ) = j(τ) − 744 = q⁻¹ + 196884q + ⋯ the normalised Hauptmodul of PSL₂(ℤ) (j = E₄³/Δ, TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms, Layer 0), t(d) = Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ} J(α_Q)/w_Q for d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4), and t(d) = 0 otherwise. The sum runs over all forms, primitive or not. *Hypotheses:* j is the normalised modular invariant E₄³/Δ (from TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms, Layer 0); J(α_Q) depends only on the class of Q. (Zagier, Traces, §1, eq. (2) and the definition of t(d), printed p. 2; Zagier, Traces, §1, table, printed p. 2.)

Its API is `modularTrace` (t(d)); `modularTrace_eq_zero` (t(d) = 0 if d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4)); `modularTrace_three` (t(3) = −248); `modularTrace_four` (t(4) = 492); `modularTrace_eq_coeff_logDeriv` (t(d) is the q-coefficient of −(2πi)⁻¹Λ_d, whose constant term is H(d) (`heegnerLogDeriv`)).

*Construction.* Define modularTrace d := Σ_{Q ∈ heegnerClasses d} (j(α_Q) − 744)/w_Q. Independence of representatives: j is PSL₂(ℤ)-invariant and α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹α_Q.

*Needs:* `heegnerForms`; Mathlib `ModularForm.E₄`; Mathlib `ModularForm.discriminant`; TauCetiRoadmap.ModularForms, Layer 0 (`JInputs`).

**Zagier's weight-3/2 form g = θ₁E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶.** Define `zagierTraceForm`. g(τ) = θ₁(τ)E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ on ℍ, with θ₁(τ) = Σ_{n∈ℤ}(−1)ⁿq^{n²} (= jacobiTheta₂(1/2, 2τ)), E₄ the normalised Eisenstein series of weight 4 and η the Dedekind eta function. It is a weakly holomorphic modular form of weight 3/2 on Γ₀(4) in Kohnen's plus space, with Fourier expansion g(τ) = Σ_{d≥−1}B(d)q^d = q⁻¹ − 2 + 248q³ − 492q⁴ + 4119q⁷ − 7256q⁸ + ⋯, where B(d) = 0 unless d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4). *Hypotheses:* The half-integral weight predicate and theta multiplier use MetaplecticAutomorphicForms Layer 7 conventions; the particular form is proved modular below from the explicit rank-one finite-Weil laws, without importing an unstated general Kohnen isomorphism. (Zagier, Traces, §1, eq. (3), printed p. 2.)

Its API is `zagierTraceForm` (g(τ) on ℍ); `zagierTraceCoeff` (B(d), the coefficient of q^d (d ≥ −1)); `hasSum_zagierTraceForm` (g(τ) = Σ_{d≥−1}B(d)q^d for τ ∈ ℍ); `zagierTraceCoeff_eq_zero` (B(d) = 0 if d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4) (Kohnen's plus condition)); `zagierTraceCoeff_neg_one` (B(−1) = 1); `zagierTraceCoeff_zero` (B(0) = −2).

*Construction.* Define zagierTraceForm τ := jacobiTheta₂ (1/2) (2τ)·E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ using Mathlib's jacobiTheta₂, ModularForm.E₄ and ModularForm.eta (η(4τ) ≠ 0 by ModularForm.eta_ne_zero). Its q-expansion: θ₁ = 1 − 2q + 2q⁴ − ⋯, E₄(4τ) = 1 + 240q⁴ + ⋯, η(4τ)^{−6} = q^{−1}(1 + 6q⁴ + ⋯); multiply. The plus condition B(d) ≠ 0 ⇒ d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4): θ₁ has exponents n² ≡ 0, 1 and E₄(4τ)/η(4τ)⁶ has exponents ≡ −1 (mod 4). For the exact finite-Weil comparison set Θ_μ(τ)=Σ_{r≡μ (mod2)}q^{r²/4}, A(τ)=E₄(τ)/η(τ)⁶, and H=(−AΘ₁,AΘ₀). Splitting g(τ/4) by exponent modulo4 gives H_μ=Σ_{d≡−μ² (mod4)}B(d)q^{d/4}; in particular g(τ)=H₀(4τ)+H₁(4τ). The discriminant module is ℤ/2ℤ with Q(μ)=μ²/4, exactly the MetaplecticAutomorphicForms §4.7.6 rank-one convention already compared in Layer 1. The theta laws are Θ(τ+1)=diag(1,i)Θ(τ) and Θ(−1/τ)=√(−iτ)FΘ(τ), F=2^{−1/2}((1,1),(1,−1)). Eta and E₄ give A(τ+1)=−iA(τ) and A(−1/τ)=−iτ A(τ). Therefore H(τ+1)=diag(1,−i)H(τ) and H(−1/τ)=τ^{3/2}e(1/8)FH(τ): the dual weight 3/2 Weil law with its phase specified. To recover the claimed scalar law on Γ₀(4), use generators T, U=(1,0;4,1), and −I. Acting on 4τ changes these to T⁴, ST⁻¹S⁻¹, and −I. The row (1,1) is fixed by the dual matrices for T⁴ and ST⁻¹S⁻¹ (the latter is F diag(1,i) F); tracking the square roots through these products gives g(τ+1)=g(τ) and g(τ/(4τ+1))=(4τ+1)^{3/2}g(τ), with the coherent −I lift. These are the usual theta-multiplier-cubed laws; the plus support is already proved. The finite vector expansion and these transforms give finite principal parts at each cusp. Thus the scalar predicate is established for this g at its full stated scope.

**The recursions for the coefficients of g (Zagier §2).** Prove `zagier_trace_form_recursions`: For every n ≥ 0: Σ_{r∈ℤ}B(4n − r²) = 0 and Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n), with σ₃(0) := 1/240 and B(d) := 0 for d < −1. These determine all B(d) recursively from B(−1) = 1: B(4n − 1) = 240σ₃(n) − Σ_{2≤r≤√(4n+1)}r²B(4n − r²) and B(4n) = −2Σ_{1≤r≤√(4n+1)}B(4n − r²). *Hypotheses:* n ≥ 0. (Zagier, Traces, §2, printed p. 3; Zagier, Traces, §2, printed p. 3; §1 equation(3), printed p. 2.)

*Proof sketch.* Use the explicit H and Θ constructed for `zagierTraceForm`. Root filtering and their opposite congruence supports give (gθ)|U₄=Σ_μ H_μΘ_μ. This is identically zero by H₀=−AΘ₁ and H₁=AΘ₀. This proves the first identity without a general scalar Kohnen/U₄ assertion. Let D=q d/dq. The same filtering gives [g,θ]|U₄=4Σ_μ((DH_μ)Θ_μ−3H_μDΘ_μ). Under S and T, the displayed dual Weil matrices statement to the identity; the derivative correction terms cancel because the weights are3/2 and 1/2. Consequently this contraction is a scalar weight 4 form for SL₂(ℤ). It is holomorphic on ℍ since η has no zeros there. Its expansion has no negative integer powers: H₁ begins q^{−1/4}, Θ₁ begins2q^{1/4}, and the other component has no pole. It is therefore holomorphic at the sole cusp. The constant of the contraction is 4((−1/4)·2−3·(1/4)·2)=−8. Since M₄(SL₂(ℤ))=ℂE₄, it equals−8E₄. Its qⁿ coefficient is Σ_r(4n−4r²)B(4n−r²)=−8Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n−r²), using the first identity. Fourier uniqueness gives the second identity, including n=0 with the stated σ₃(0). Solve the r=1 and r=0 terms to obtain the recursions. Every other index is smaller than the index being determined; the support and B(−1),B(0) therefore determine the entire sequence.

**The weight-two logarithmic derivative Λ_d of the class polynomial.** Define `heegnerLogDeriv`. For d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4): Λ_d(τ) = Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}(1/w_Q)·j′(τ)/(j(τ) − j(α_Q)), a meromorphic modular form of weight 2 on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with a simple pole at each α ∈ ℍ satisfying a quadratic equation over ℤ of discriminant −d, of residue 1 as a function on ℍ (Zagier's ‘residue 1/|Γ_α|’ is the residue of Λ_d dτ in the local coordinate of the quotient curve, which differs by the factor |Γ_α| at the elliptic points i and ρ), and with q-expansion −(2πi)⁻¹Λ_d = H(d) + t(d)q + O(q²). It is the logarithmic derivative of H_d(j(τ)) = ∏(j(τ) − j(α_Q))^{1/w_Q}, and it is uniquely characterised among forms with at most simple poles by its poles and residues because M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0. *Hypotheses:* j′ = dj/dτ; Λ_d avoids the fractional powers in H_d. (Zagier, Traces, §4, definition of Λ_d, printed p. 5; Zagier, Traces, §3, eq. (11), printed p. 4.)

Its API is `heegnerLogDeriv` (Λ_d(τ)); `heegnerLogDeriv_slash` (Λ_d is invariant under the weight-2 slash action of SL₂(ℤ)); `heegnerLogDeriv_qExpansion` (−(2πi)⁻¹Λ_d = H(d) + t(d)q + O(q²) as Im τ → ∞); `heegnerLogDeriv_residue` (Λ_d has a simple pole of residue 1 (as a function on ℍ) at each CM point α of discriminant −d and no other poles in ℍ; at the elliptic points this is j − j(α) vanishing to order |Γ_α| times the weight 1/w_Q = 1/|Γ_α|); `heegnerLogDeriv_unique` (A meromorphic weight-2 form with at most simple poles on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with the same poles and residues as a combination of the Λ_d, equals that combination).

*Construction.* Define heegnerLogDeriv d τ := Σ_{Q ∈ heegnerClasses d} (1/w_Q)·deriv j τ/(j τ − j α_Q). Modularity of weight 2: j′ has weight 2 and j is invariant. Residues: j − j(α_Q) vanishes at α_Q to order |Γ_{α_Q}| = w_Q (to order 2 at i, since j − 1728 = E₆²/Δ, and to order 3 at ρ, since j = E₄³/Δ), so (1/w_Q)j′/(j − j(α_Q)) has residue 1. Expansion at ∞: −(2πi)^{−1}j′ = q^{−1} − 196884q + ⋯ and j − j(α) = q^{−1} − J(α) + O(q), so each term is 1 + J(α_Q)q + O(q²). Uniqueness: two meromorphic weight-2 forms with the same principal parts differ by a holomorphic weight-2 form, which is 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

**The logarithmic derivative of Φ_n(j, j) (Zagier (9)).** Prove `modular_diagonal_log_derivative`: For n≥1 let M_n be all integral determinant-n matrices, not just primitive ones, and D_n(τ)=∏_{ad=n, a,d>0}∏_{0≤b<d}(j(τ)−j((aτ+b)/d)). For nonsquare n, D′_n/D_n=Σ_{|r|<2√n}Λ_{4n−r²}. For n=m² omit the single identically zero scalar-coset factor (a,d,b)=(m,m,0), obtaining D_n*. Then (D_n*)′/D_n*=Σ_{|r|<2√n}Λ_{4n−r²}−Λ₄−2Λ₃. These are meromorphic weight 2 identities on ℍ. The all-matrix product is sometimes denoted Φ_n(j,j); a convention that reserves Φ_n for primitive matrices must instead use the corresponding product of primitive modular polynomials. *Hypotheses:* n ≥ 1; the square case as stated. (Zagier, Traces, §3, eqs. (8)–(9), printed pp. 3–4; Zagier, Traces, §3, equations(8)–(11), printed pp. 3–4.)

*Proof sketch.* Integer row reduction gives unique representatives (a,b;0,d), ad=n, a,d>0,0≤b<d for SL₂(ℤ)\M_n. Right multiplication permutes them, proving invariance of the finite product. This uses the full determinant-n coset set, including nonprimitive matrices. Its logarithmic derivative is weight 2 and its finite Laurent expansion at ∞ is bounded. If j(α)=j(Mα), injectivity of j on Γ\ℍ supplies a left translate N fixing α. For N=(a,b;c,d), tr N=r, choose the sign c>0 and associate Q=[c,d−a,−b]; its discriminant is r²−4n. Conversely Q=[A,B,C] and r with B≡r mod2 give N=((r−B)/2,−C;A,(r+B)/2). Discriminant equality implies this parity condition. This is the exact fixed-matrix/quadratic-form dictionary, with imprimitive Q retained. Write t=(τ−α)/(τ−conjugate α), w=|Γ_α|, λ=cα+d, s=n/λ². Then t(Nτ)=s t and j(τ)=j(α)+c₀t^w+O(t^{2w}), c₀≠0. Unless s^w=1, a fixing branch j(τ)−j(Nτ) has zero of order w. The condition s^w=1 means precisely that N is a scalar times an element of Γ_α, hence is the omitted scalar coset and requires n square. Each remaining left coset fixing α has exactly w fixing representatives modulo sign. The Q,r dictionary thus counts w labels for each zero of order w. Each corresponding Λ has residue1 on ℍ. This proves equality of all residues, also at i and ρ. For n=m² the identity coset mΓ has w−1 nonscalar stabilizer matrices at an elliptic point; their Q are multiples by m of the basic elliptic forms and have the same j values. Their contribution is exactly Λ₄+2Λ₃, independently of m. Remove these along with the scalar branch. In particular D₁*=1 and the right side is 0. No other poles occur; after cancelling these principal parts the difference is holomorphic in ℍ and at ∞, hence belongs to M₂(SL₂(ℤ))=0. This proves both formulas.

E₄ has order w−2 there, so E₄(Nτ)/E₄(τ) tends to s^{w−2}. The residue is therefore−wn s^w/(2πi(1−s^w)). Pairing s with s⁻¹ gives wn/(2πi). ### Examples

- Kontsevich's function at roots of unity: F(1) = 1, F(−1) = 3, F(i) = 8 − 3i.
- The five partitions 4, 3 + 1, 2 + 2, 2 + 1 + 1 and 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 have cranks 4, 0, 2, −2 and −4, one in each residue class modulo 5, as the crank explanation of p(5n + 4) ≡ 0 (mod 5) requires at n = 0.
- t(3) = (j(ρ) − 744)/3 = −248 and t(4) = (j(i) − 744)/2 = 492, and g(τ) = q⁻¹ − 2 + 248q³ − 492q⁴ + ⋯, whose coefficient of q^d is −t(d).
- Hurwitz class numbers: H(3) = 1/3, H(4) = 1/2, H(12) = 4/3, the weighted counts of §5.8.

## Layer 6: Vertex algebras, the Monster Lie algebra and moonshine

This layer builds Borcherds' proof of monstrous moonshine. Vertex algebras are defined over an arbitrary commutative ring by the Borcherds identity, with their Lie quotient, existence theorem, tensor products, conformal vectors, vertex operator algebras, invariant forms and graded traces; the vertex algebra of an even lattice is constructed for every signature. For a vertex algebra with conformal vector of central charge 26 the physical states form a Lie algebra, and the no-ghost theorem identifies its root spaces. Borcherds algebras are characterised and their free subalgebras described; applied to the moonshine module tensored with the lattice vertex algebra of II₁,₁ this gives the Monster Lie algebra, its simple roots and its twisted denominator identities, hence complete replicability of the McKay–Thompson series. With the formal theory of j, Hecke operators and Hauptmoduln this proves that every McKay–Thompson series of the moonshine module is the normalised Hauptmodul of a genus-zero group.

Standing assumptions: vertex algebras are over a commutative ring R unless a field of characteristic zero is required; graded pieces of vertex operator algebras are finite-dimensional when traces are taken; modular functions are on ℍ with Laurent expansions at ∞.

### 6.1 Vertex algebras

**Vertex algebra (Borcherds' axioms).** The definition follows the shape of Mathlib's vertex-algebra development (`Mathlib/Algebra/Vertex`, with the open Mathlib pull request 25822 of the same author for the full axioms), over an arbitrary commutative ring. AffineLieAlgebras A6 (vacuum vertex algebras of affine Lie algebras over a field of characteristic zero) and C7 (positive-definite lattice vertex algebras over ℂ) are instances, compared in the API below. Define `VertexAlgebra.nprod`. Let R be a commutative ring and V an R-module. A vertex algebra structure on V is a pair (Y, 1) with Y : V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V (Mathlib's vertex operators: R-linear maps from V to Laurent series in z with coefficients in V, support bounded below) and a vacuum vector 1 ∈ V. Write u_n := VertexOperator.ncoeff (Y u) n ∈ End_R(V), so that Y(u,z) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} u_n z^{−n−1}. The axioms are: (creation) u_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0 and u_{−1} 1 = u; (Borcherds identity) for all u, v, w ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ, Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_{q+i} v)_{m+n−i} w = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{m+q−i}(v_{n+i} w) − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i}(u_{m+i} w) ), where C(m,i) = m(m−1)⋯(m−i+1)/i! ∈ ℤ is Mathlib's Ring.choose m i. The truncation axiom (for u, v there is N with u_n v = 0 for all n ≥ N) holds automatically because the support of Y(u,z)v is bounded below in z; hence both sums in the Borcherds identity are finite. Convention: index n of u_n is the 'mode' of Borcherds and Matsuo–Nagatomo; (u_n) for n ≥ 0 are the annihilation modes. *Hypotheses:* R is a commutative ring. V is an R-module. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 12; Matsuo–Nagatomo, Definition 3.1.1, p. 21–22; Borcherds 1986, §4, p. 3–4.)

Its API is `VertexAlgebra.nprod` (The n-th product u_n v := VertexOperator.ncoeff (Y u) n v, R-bilinear in (u, v)); `VertexAlgebra.nprod_eq_zero_of_le` (Truncation: for all u, v there is N : ℤ with u_n v = 0 for all n ≥ N); `VertexAlgebra.nprod_vac_of_nonneg` (u_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0); `VertexAlgebra.nprod_vac_neg_one` (u_{−1} 1 = u); `VertexAlgebra.borcherds_identity` (The Borcherds identity in the form above, with both sides finite sums over ℕ); `VertexAlgebra.ext` (Two vertex algebra structures on V with equal Y and equal vacuum are equal); `VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation` (For a commutative ℚ-algebra A and a derivation ∂ of A, the vertex algebra with u_n v = (∂^{−n−1}u/(−n−1)!)v for n ≤ −1 and 0 for n ≥ 0, vacuum 1); `VertexAlgebra.toFormalVertexAxioms` (Over ℂ, a vertex algebra in this sense with translation T(u) := u_{−2}1 gives an instance of AffineLieAlgebras C7's `FormalVertexAxioms` on the same space with the same field (u_n = coefficient of z^{−n−1} in both conventions), and C7's `formalVertex_borcherds` gives the converse; the two notions agree over ℂ. The definition here is the general one (any commutative ring), needed for the integral Lie quotient of `VertexAlgebra.translationSpan` and the real moonshine model).

*Construction.* Package the data as a structure whose field Y has type V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V and whose field vac is the vacuum; the two creation equations and the Borcherds identity are Prop fields stated with VertexOperator.ncoeff and Ring.choose. Truncation: HVertexOperator.coeff_isPWOsupport gives that the support of the Laurent series Y(u,z)v is partially well ordered, hence bounded below in ℤ; since VertexOperator.ncoeff A n = HVertexOperator.coeff A (−n−1) (VertexOperator.ncoeff_apply), u_n v = 0 for n large. Finiteness of the sums: the i-th term on the left vanishes once q+i exceeds the truncation bound of (u,v); on the right once n+i and m+i exceed the bounds of (v,w) and (u,w). State the identity with finite sums over ℕ (finsum) and record the finiteness as an API lemma. Comparison with AffineLieAlgebras C7 (TauCetiRoadmap pull request #1201) over ℂ: the vacuum, creation and translation axioms of C7's `FormalVertexAxioms` follow from the Borcherds identity with T(u) = u_{−2}1 (Matsuo–Nagatomo §§1–2), locality is the case m ≥ N of the identity, and conversely C7's `formalVertex_borcherds` derives the Borcherds identity from its axioms; the coefficient conventions coincide.

*Needs:* Mathlib `VertexOperator`; Mathlib `VertexOperator.ncoeff`; Mathlib `HVertexOperator.coeff`; Mathlib `Ring.choose`; Mathlib `BinomialRing`; TauCetiRoadmap.AffineLieAlgebras C7.

**Checks.**

- In VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation for A = ℚ[X] and ∂ = d/dX: X_{−2}1 = 1, X_{−1}X = X² and X_n X = 0 for n ≥ 0.
- On the zero module there is exactly one vertex algebra structure (Y = 0, vacuum 0).
- For the non-commutative ring M₂(ℚ), the rule u_n v := δ_{n,−1}uv with vacuum 1 violates the Borcherds identity (with m = −1, n = 0, q = −1 and w = 1 it forces uv = vu for the matrix units u = E₁₂, v = E₂₁).
- In VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation every product u_n v with n ≥ 0 vanishes and u_{−1}v = uv, so the commutative algebra is recovered from the (−1)-product.
- Over ℂ, for VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation on ℂ[X] with ∂ = d/dX, the associated C7 FormalVertexAxioms has translation d/dX, and the coefficients of z⁰, z¹, z² in the field of X applied to 1 are X, 1 and 0, as its creation axiom (1/n!)Tⁿ requires.

**Vacuum, translation and derivation rules in a vertex algebra.** Prove `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation`: Let (V, Y, 1) be a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R. Define D : V → V by D v := v_{−2}1 and, for k ≥ 0, D^{(k)} v := v_{−k−1}1. Then: (a) 1_n v = δ_{n,−1} v for all n (Y(1,z) = id); (b) D 1 = 0; (c) (Dv)_n = −n v_{n−1} for all n; (d) [D, v_n] = −n v_{n−1}, i.e. D(v_n w) = (Dv)_n w + v_n(Dw), so D is a derivation of every product; (e) k·D^{(k)} v = D(D^{(k−1)} v) for k ≥ 1, hence k!·D^{(k)} = D^k; (f) u_n 1 = D^{(−n−1)} u for n ≤ −1. *Hypotheses:* (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra over R. (Matsuo–Nagatomo, §3.1, equations (18)–(22), p. 22–23; Borcherds 1986, §4, relations (ii), (iii), p. 3.)

*Proof sketch.* (b): put u = v = w = 1 and m = n = q = −1 in the Borcherds identity (Matsuo–Nagatomo (18)). (e),(f): put v = w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n; the creation axiom gives (u_n 1)_{−2}1 = −n u_{n−1}1, which is (e) after reindexing (Matsuo–Nagatomo (19)). (a): put v = w = 1, m = −1, n = q', q = 0 and use (b) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (20)). (c): put v = 1, m = n', n = 0, q = −2 and use (a) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (21)). (d): put w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n (Matsuo–Nagatomo (22)); compare with (c).

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`.

**Checks.**

- In VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation, D is the given derivation ∂.
- Over a ℚ-algebra, Y(u,z)1 = e^{zD}u as formal power series.

**Commutator and associativity formulas.** Prove `vertex_algebra_commutator_formula`: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring, for all u, v ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ: (commutator formula) [u_m, v_n] = Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_i v)_{m+n−i}; (associativity formula, applied to each w) (u_q v)_n w = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{q−i}(v_{n+i}w) − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i}(u_iw) ) as a pointwise finite sum in V. The associativity sum need not have finite support as a family of endomorphisms; only its evaluation at each w is finitely supported. In particular [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n, so u ↦ u_0 acts by derivations of all products. *Hypotheses:* (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra. (Matsuo–Nagatomo, §3.2, formulas (25), (26), p. 24; Borcherds 1986, §8, p. 8.)

*Proof sketch.* Set q = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the right side is u_m v_n w − v_n u_m w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (25)). Set m = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the left side is (u_q v)_n w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (26)). Keep w explicit in the finite sum: truncation bounds depend on w, so finsum in End(V) is not justified. For m = 0 the commutator formula reads [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; Mathlib `Ring.choose`.

**Checks.**

- For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation all commutators vanish, consistent with u_i v = 0 for i ≥ 0.
- Borcherds 1986 §8 states the commutator formula [u_m, v_n] = Σ_j C(m,j)(u_j v)_{m+n−j}.

**Skew symmetry.** Prove `vertex_algebra_skew_symmetry`: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R, for all u, v ∈ V and n ∈ ℤ: v_n u = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^{n+i+1} D^{(i)}(u_{n+i} v), where D^{(i)}x := x_{−i−1}1 (a finite sum by truncation). In particular v_0 u + u_0 v = Σ_{i≥1} (−1)^{i+1} D^{(i)}(u_i v) lies in the R-span DV_div := Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V), and, when2 is invertible in R, u_0 u∈DV_div by dividing the self-skew identity by 2. The arbitrary-ring alternating conclusion requires a further argument, not this division. *Hypotheses:* (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra. (Matsuo–Nagatomo, §3.1, formula (23), p. 23; Borcherds 1986, §4, relation (iv), p. 3.)

*Proof sketch.* Put w = 1, m = −1, n = 0, q = n in the Borcherds identity and simplify with the creation axiom and the vacuum-translation lemma (Matsuo–Nagatomo (23)). For n = 0 separate the i = 0 term: v_0 u = −u_0 v + Σ_{i≥1}(−1)^{i+1}D^{(i)}(u_i v).

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation`.

**Checks.**

- For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation with n = −1 the identity is v u = u v + (terms with ∂), i.e. commutativity of A.
- Borcherds 1986 §4 takes this as axiom (iv).

**The universal Lie quotient of a vertex algebra.** Define `VertexAlgebra.translationSpan`. Let V be a vertex algebra over an arbitrary commutative ring R and let DV be the R-span of D^{(i)}w for i≥1. The zero product descends to an anticommutative Leibniz bracket on Q=V/DV. Its square submodule A=span_R{[x,x]:x∈Q} is central and annihilated by 2. Consequently LieQuotient(V):=Q/A, equivalently V/(DV+span_R{u₀u}), is a Lie algebra over R, universal among R-linear bracket-preserving maps from Q to Lie algebras. Zero modes make V a module over this Lie quotient and act by derivations of every vertex product. If2 is invertible in R, A=0 and the canonical map Q→LieQuotient(V) is an isomorphism, recovering V/DV in every moonshine application here. When2 is not invertible, Q itself need not be alternating: the integral neutral fermion reduced modulo2, described below, has a nonzero self-bracket in Q. *Hypotheses:* V is a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R. (Borcherds 1986, §4, p. 4; Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 12; Kac–Wang 1993, §4, printed pp. 37–38, free-fermion Fock construction before Theorem 4.1.)

Its API is `VertexAlgebra.translationSpan` (The submodule DV = Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V) of V); `VertexAlgebra.LieQuotient` (The module V/(DV+span_R{u₀u}), with alternating LieRing and LieAlgebra R structures induced by zero products); `VertexAlgebra.LieQuotient.bracket_mk` (⁅mk u, mk v⁆ = mk (u_0 v)); `VertexAlgebra.zeroMode_translation` ((D^{(i)} w)_0 = 0 for i ≥ 1); `VertexAlgebra.lieModuleQuotient` (V is a LieModule over LieQuotient(V), via mk(u)·w=u₀w; both divided translations and square products act by zero); `VertexAlgebra.zeroMode_derivation` (u_0(v_n w) = (u_0 v)_n w + v_n(u_0 w)); `VertexAlgebra.squareSpan` (The central submodule A=span_R{[x,x]} of the anticommutative Leibniz quotient Q=V/DV; multiplication by 2 annihilates A); `VertexAlgebra.LieQuotient.lift` (Every R-linear bracket-preserving map Q→L to an alternating R-Lie algebra L factors uniquely through Q/A); `VertexAlgebra.LieQuotient.ofTwoIsUnit` (If2 is a unit in R, the canonical map V/DV→LieQuotient(V) is an R-linear bracket equivalence, compatible with zero-mode actions).

*Construction.* Extract the divided translation identity (D^{(i)}u)_n=(−1)^i binomial(n,i)u_{n−i} directly from the vacuum specialization of the Borcherds identity, not by dividing an iterated D formula by i!. At n=0 every i≥1 gives zero. The zero-mode derivation formula applied to u_{−i−1}1 gives v₀D^{(i)}u=D^{(i)}(v₀u), since v₀1=0. Thus DV is a two-sided zero-product ideal and acts trivially by zero modes. Skew symmetry gives u₀v+v₀u∈DV. The commutator formula at m=n=0 gives [u,[v,w]]−[v,[u,w]]=[[u,v],w]. Hence Q has the stated anticommutative Leibniz bracket. Setting v=u shows [[u,u],w]=0, and anticommutativity gives [w,[u,u]]=0. Thus A is central. Also2[u,u]=0. Quotient by A is alternating and satisfies Jacobi; the universal property is the linear quotient property because every map to an alternating Lie algebra kills A. The zero-mode action kills each square as well: (u₀u)₀=[u₀,u₀]=0 as endomorphisms. It therefore factors through the actual Lie quotient and gives the Lie-module identity. Each endomorphism u₀ is a derivation of all vertex products by `vertex_algebra_commutator_formula`. If2 is invertible, the equation2A=0 gives A=0 and proves the comparison, without a change to any real moonshine construction. The need for A over arbitrary rings has an explicit witness. Start with the integral neutral-fermion super Fock module F_ℤ=Λ_ℤ(x₀,x₁,…). Let a_{−j−1} be exterior multiplication by x_j and a_j contraction by x_j, j≥0. Their anticommutator is δ_{m+n,−1}; a=a_{−1}1 has a₀a=1. The normal-ordered fields and Hasse derivatives in Kac–Wang §4 have integral binomial coefficients and preserve this free ℤ-module. Their super vertex identities hold overℚ and therefore overℤ by torsion-free coefficient comparison. Reduction modulo2 removes all super signs and gives an ordinary vertex algebra over𝔽₂. Give x_j degree j+1/2. All degrees are nonnegative, only1 has degree 0, D^{(i)} raises degree by i, and D^{(i)}1=0 for i>0. Consequently 1∉DV, while a₀a=1. Thus Q fails alternation. So the quotient by DV alone is not a Lie algebra over such a ring, and the alternating quotient is required.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation`; `vertex_algebra_commutator_formula`; `vertex_algebra_skew_symmetry`; Mathlib `LieAlgebra`; Mathlib `LieModule`.

**Checks.**

- For a commutative differential vertex algebra all zero products vanish, so A=0 and LieQuotient is the abelian module V/DV.
- The bracket of every element with itself vanishes in the universal Lie quotient over every R, even when2=0.
- Over ℝ the natural quotient map V/DV→LieQuotient is an isomorphism intertwining zero-mode actions; this is the carrier used by physical-state and Monster-Lie constructions.
- For the reduced integral neutral fermion over𝔽₂, a₀a=1 and 1∉DV. Hence V/DV has a nonzero self-bracket, while the image of 1 in LieQuotient is zero.

**Homomorphisms and automorphisms of vertex algebras.** Define `VertexAlgebra.Hom`. For vertex algebras (V, Y, 1) and (W, Y', 1') over R, a homomorphism is an R-linear map f : V → W with f(1) = 1' and f(u_n v) = f(u)_n f(v) for all u, v, n (equivalently f ∘ Y(u,z) = Y'(f u, z) ∘ f). The automorphisms of V form a group Aut(V) under composition. If V carries a conformal vector ω (statement conformal-vector) the conformal automorphisms are those with g(ω) = ω; if V carries a bilinear form (,) the isometric conformal automorphisms are those with (gu, gv) = (u, v). For a group G, an action of G on V by vertex algebra automorphisms is a group homomorphism G →* Aut(V). *Hypotheses:* V, W vertex algebras over the same commutative ring R. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 14; Jurisich 2009, §3, Theorem 1 (3), p. 5.)

Its API is `VertexAlgebra.Hom` (Homomorphisms f with f 1 = 1 and f(u_n v) = (f u)_n (f v)); `VertexAlgebra.Hom.map_nprod` (f (u_n v) = (f u)_n (f v)); `VertexAlgebra.Aut` (Aut(V) is a group under composition); `VertexAlgebra.Aut.commute_translation` (g ∘ D = D ∘ g for g ∈ Aut(V)); `VertexAlgebra.Aut.conformal` (The subgroup of g ∈ Aut(V) with g ω = ω (for V with conformal vector ω)); `VertexAlgebra.Aut.mapsTo_weightSpace` (A conformal automorphism maps each L_0-eigenspace V_n into itself).

*Construction.* Define VertexAlgebra.Hom as a structure extending V →ₗ[R] W with the two compatibility fields; composition and identity are immediate. Define Aut(V) as the group of invertible homomorphisms (bundled as R-linear equivalences satisfying the two conditions); the inverse of a bijective homomorphism is a homomorphism. Define the subgroups of conformal and of conformal isometric automorphisms as stabilizers.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; Mathlib `LinearMap.BilinForm`.

**Checks.**

- The identity automorphism acts as the identity on V and fixes 1.
- The automorphism group of the zero vertex algebra is trivial.
- If2 is invertible in R and V is nonzero, v↦−v is not a vertex algebra homomorphism: creation makes the vacuum nonzero, and −1≠1. In characteristic2, negation is the identity and is a homomorphism.
- For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation A ∂, an R-algebra automorphism σ of A with σ∂ = ∂σ is a vertex algebra automorphism.

**Existence theorem for vertex algebras (locality criterion).** Prove `vertex_algebra_existence_theorem`: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, V a k-vector space, 1 ∈ V nonzero, T ∈ End_k(V), and S a set of fields on V (formal series A(z) = Σ A_n z^{−n−1} with A_n ∈ End(V) and A(z)w ∈ V((z)) for every w) such that: (S1) the fields in S are pairwise local: for A, B ∈ S there is N with (y−z)^N [A(y), B(z)] = 0; (S2) the vectors A^{λ1}_{−j1−1}⋯A^{λk}_{−jk−1}1 (k ≥ 0, j_i ≥ 0, A^{λi} ∈ S) span V; (S3) each A ∈ S is creative (A_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0) and translation covariant: [T, A(z)] = ∂_z A(z), with T1 = 0. Then there is a unique vertex algebra structure on V with vacuum 1 such that Y(A_{−1}1, z) = A(z) for every A ∈ S; its translation operator is T. *Hypotheses:* k field of characteristic 0. S pairwise local, creative, translation covariant, generating V from 1. (Matsuo–Nagatomo, Theorem 5.4.1 (Existence theorem), p. 35; Bakalov–Kac 2006, Corollary 3.3, §3.)

*Proof sketch.* Let O be the space of creative fields; the residual products A(z)_{(m)}B(z) of local fields are local (Dong's lemma, Matsuo–Nagatomo Proposition 1.5.5) and creative (Lemma 4.1.2). The space ⟨S⟩ of fields generated by S under residual products is pairwise local and contains the identity field; by Li's theorem (Matsuo–Nagatomo Theorem 3.3.1, via the Borcherds identity for local fields, Corollary 2.2.2 and Theorem 2.4.1) it is a vertex algebra. Translation covariance and (S2) make the state map A(z) ↦ A_{−1}1 bijective from ⟨S⟩ onto V (Theorem 5.3.3); transport the structure along it. Uniqueness: a vertex algebra structure is determined by the fields of a generating set, by the associativity formula (`vertex_algebra_commutator_formula`). Over k = ℂ this is the reconstruction phase (i) of AffineLieAlgebras C7 (TauCetiRoadmap pull request #1201), transported through the comparison of `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; the statement here, over every field of characteristic 0, is the generality the real framed moonshine model of `monster_head_characters` (§6.10) needs, and it agrees with C7's after extension of scalars to ℂ.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation`; `vertex_algebra_commutator_formula`; Mathlib `VertexOperator`; TauCetiRoadmap.AffineLieAlgebras C7.

**Checks.**

- The vertex algebra structure of VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation is recovered from S = {Y(a, z) : a ∈ A} with T = ∂.
- Applied to S = {Y(a⊗1), Y(1⊗b)} it produces the tensor product vertex algebra (`VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct`).

**Tensor product of vertex algebras.** Define `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct`. Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0. The k-vector space V ⊗_k W carries a unique vertex algebra structure with vacuum 1 ⊗ 1 and (a ⊗ b)_n (c ⊗ d) = Σ_{i∈ℤ} (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d) (a finite sum by truncation), i.e. Y(a⊗b, z) = Y(a,z) ⊗ Y(b,z). The maps a ↦ a ⊗ 1 and b ↦ 1 ⊗ b are vertex algebra homomorphisms whose images commute: [(a⊗1)_m, (1⊗b)_n] = 0. *Hypotheses:* V, W vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Jurisich 1998, §6.1, p. 30.)

Its API is `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct` (The vertex algebra structure on V ⊗[k] W with vacuum 1 ⊗ 1); `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct_nprod_tmul` ((a ⊗ b)_n (c ⊗ d) = Σ_i (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d)); `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct.inl` (a ↦ a ⊗ 1 is a vertex algebra homomorphism V → V ⊗ W); `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct.inr` (b ↦ 1 ⊗ b is a vertex algebra homomorphism W → V ⊗ W); `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct.map` (Homomorphisms f : V → V', g : W → W' induce f ⊗ g : V ⊗ W → V' ⊗ W'; in particular Aut(V) acts on V ⊗ W through the first factor); `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct_translation` (D_{V⊗W} = D_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_W).

*Construction.* Define the fields Y(a⊗1, z) := Y(a,z) ⊗ id and Y(1⊗b, z) := id ⊗ Y(b,z) on V ⊗ W; they are creative for 1⊗1 and translation covariant for T := D_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_W. Locality: fields from the same factor are local by locality in V or W (Matsuo–Nagatomo (27)); fields from different factors commute. The products (a⊗1)_{−1}(1⊗b)_{−1}(1⊗1) = a⊗b span, so the existence theorem gives the vertex algebra; normal ordering identifies Y(a⊗b, z) with Y(a,z)⊗Y(b,z), which yields the displayed formula for the modes. The two inclusions are homomorphisms by uniqueness in the existence theorem.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod`; `vertex_algebra_existence_theorem`; `VertexAlgebra.Hom`.

**Checks.**

- (1 ⊗ 1)_n = δ_{n,−1} id on V ⊗ W, and (a ⊗ 1)_{−1}(1 ⊗ b) = a ⊗ b.
- For the one-dimensional vertex algebra k, V ⊗ k ≃ V as vertex algebras.
- [(a⊗1)_m, (1⊗b)_n] = 0 for all a, b, m, n.
- The shifted rule (a⊗b)_n(c⊗d) := Σ_i (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−i} d) violates the creation axiom: (a⊗b)_{−1}(1⊗1) = 0, because a_i 1 ≠ 0 forces i ≤ −1 while b_{−1−i}1 ≠ 0 forces i ≥ 0; with the correct index n−1−i only i = −1 survives and gives a⊗b.

### 6.2 Conformal structure and graded traces

**The Virasoro algebra and modules of given central charge.** Define `Virasoro`. Let k be a field of characteristic 0. The Virasoro algebra Vir_k is the Lie algebra over k with basis {L_n : n ∈ ℤ} ∪ {C} and bracket [L_m, L_n] = (m − n) L_{m+n} + ((m³ − m)/12) δ_{m+n,0} C, [C, x] = 0 for all x. For c ∈ k, a Virasoro module of central charge c is a Lie module M over Vir_k on which C acts as multiplication by c; equivalently a family of operators L_n ∈ End(M) with [L_m, L_n] = (m−n)L_{m+n} + c(m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0}. *Hypotheses:* k field of characteristic 0 (the coefficient 1/12 must make sense) (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Jurisich 1998, Definition 4, (V8), p. 26.)

Its API is `Virasoro` (The Lie algebra Vir_k with its LieRing and LieAlgebra k instances); `Virasoro.L` (The basis elements L_n, n ∈ ℤ); `Virasoro.C` (The central element C); `Virasoro.lie_L_L` (⁅L m, L n⁆ = (m − n) • L (m + n) + (if m + n = 0 then (m³ − m)/12 else 0) • C); `Virasoro.lie_C` (⁅C, x⁆ = 0); `Virasoro.basis` (The k-basis indexed by ℤ ⊕ Unit); `Virasoro.isSl2Triple` (IsSl2Triple (2 • L 0) (L (−1)) (−L 1), relating to Mathlib's sl₂ theory); `Virasoro.HasCentralCharge` (A Lie module M has central charge c when C acts on M as c • id).

*Construction.* Define Vir_k as the k-module with basis ℤ ⊕ {C} (Finsupp) and the bracket extended bilinearly; check antisymmetry ((m³−m) is odd in m) and the Jacobi identity on basis elements (the cocycle ψ(m,n) = (m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0} satisfies the 2-cocycle identity). Define the module predicate as a LieModule together with the scalar action of C.

*Needs:* Mathlib `LieAlgebra`; Mathlib `LieModule`; Mathlib `IsSl2Triple`.

**Checks.**

- ⁅L 2, L (−2)⁆ = 4 • L 0 + (1/2) • C.
- ⁅L 1, L (−1)⁆ = 2 • L 0 (no central term).
- The trivial one-dimensional module has central charge 0.
- C ∈ ⁅Vir, Vir⁆ (C = 2(⁅L 2, L (−2)⁆ − 2⁅L 1, L (−1)⁆)), so Vir is not isomorphic to the split extension of the Witt algebra by k with a trivial cocycle.

**Conformal vector of a vertex algebra.** Define `ConformalVector.L`. Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with translation D (`vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation` (§6.1)). A conformal vector of central charge c ∈ k is ω ∈ V such that: ω_0 v = Dv for all v; ω_1 ω = 2ω; ω_2 ω = 0; ω_3 ω = (c/2)·1; ω_i ω = 0 for i ≥ 4; and L_0 := ω_1 is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues: V = ⊕_{n∈ℤ} V_n (internal direct sum) with V_n := ker(L_0 − n). Put L_n := ω_{n+1}. The eigenvalue n of v ∈ V_n is its (conformal) weight. Convention (Borcherds): in the moonshine module the space of weight n + 1 is Borcherds' V_n (degree n). *Hypotheses:* V vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0. c ∈ k. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 12–13.)

Its API is `ConformalVector.L` (L n := ω_{n+1} ∈ End_k(V)); `ConformalVector.L_neg_one` (L (−1) = D); `ConformalVector.weightSpace` (V_n := ker(L_0 − n) for n ∈ ℤ); `ConformalVector.isInternal_weightSpace` (V = ⊕_{n∈ℤ} V_n (DirectSum.IsInternal)); `ConformalVector.nprod_mem_weightSpace` (u ∈ V_a, v ∈ V_b ⇒ u_n v ∈ V_{a+b−n−1}); `ConformalVector.vac_mem_weightSpace_zero` (1 ∈ V_0 and ω ∈ V_2); `ConformalVector.centralCharge` (The central charge c).

*Construction.* Structure with fields ω, c and the six conditions, the last as DirectSum.IsInternal of the eigenspaces Module.End.eigenspace L_0 (n : k), n ∈ ℤ.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod` (§6.1); `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation` (§6.1); Mathlib `Module.End.eigenspace`; Mathlib `DirectSum.IsInternal`.

**Checks.**

- For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation A 0, ω = 0 is a conformal vector of central charge 0 and V = V_0.
- In the lattice vertex algebra of ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2, ω = ¼ α(−1)²1 is a conformal vector of central charge 1 and L_0 e^α = e^α.
- In the same vertex algebra, 2ω is not a conformal vector: (2ω)_1(2ω) = 8ω ≠ 2·(2ω).
- ω ∈ V_2, L_0 1 = 0 and L_{−1}ω = Dω.

**Modes of a conformal vector form a Virasoro module.** Prove `conformal_vector_virasoro_representation`: Let ω be a conformal vector of central charge c in a vertex algebra V over a field of characteristic 0, and L_n := ω_{n+1}. Then (a) [L_m, L_n] = (m − n)L_{m+n} + c (m³ − m)/12 δ_{m+n,0} for all m, n ∈ ℤ, so V is a Virasoro module of central charge c; (b) L_{−1} = D; (c) for v ∈ V_h with L_n v = 0 for all n > 0 (a primary vector of weight h), [L_m, v_n] = ((m+1)(h−1) − n) v_{m+n}; in particular for v ∈ P^1 (h = 1), [L_m, v_0] = 0, so v_0 commutes with the Virasoro action; (d) (L_{−1}v)_n = −n v_{n−1}. *Hypotheses:* ω conformal vector of central charge c. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Borcherds 1986, §5, p. 5.)

*Proof sketch.* (a): apply the commutator formula [ω_{m+1}, ω_{n+1}] = Σ_i C(m+1,i)(ω_i ω)_{m+n+2−i} and substitute ω_0 ω = Dω, ω_1ω = 2ω, ω_2ω = 0, ω_3ω = (c/2)1, ω_iω = 0 (i ≥ 4), with (Dω)_k = −k ω_{k−1} and 1_k = δ_{k,−1}. (b) is the axiom ω_0 = D. (c): commutator formula [ω_{m+1}, v_n] = Σ_i C(m+1,i) (ω_i v)_{m+n+1−i}; for primary v, ω_i v = L_{i−1} v vanishes for i ≥ 2, ω_1 v = hv and ω_0 v = Dv, and (Dv)_k = −k v_{k−1}. (d) is the vacuum-translation lemma (c).

*Needs:* `ConformalVector.L`; `vertex_algebra_commutator_formula` (§6.1); `vertex_algebra_vacuum_translation` (§6.1); `Virasoro`.

**Checks.**

- For the rank-d lattice vertex algebra the central charge is d (Borcherds 1986 §5).
- Borcherds 1986 §5: [L_j, u_k] = ((j+1)(i−1) − k)u_{j+k} for u ∈ P^i (the source prints P^1).

**Vertex operator algebra.** Define `VertexOperatorAlgebra`. A vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 is a vertex algebra V over k with a conformal vector ω of central charge c such that each weight space V_n = ker(L_0 − n) is finite-dimensional and V_n = 0 for all sufficiently negative n (V = ⊕_{n ≥ N} V_n). It is nonnegatively graded when V_n = 0 for n < 0 (Borcherds' definition: all L_0-eigenvalues are nonnegative integers), and of CFT type when moreover 1 ≠ 0 and V_0 = k·1 (a one-dimensional vacuum space). A homomorphism of vertex operator algebras is a vertex algebra homomorphism sending ω to ω; Aut(V, ω) is the group of conformal automorphisms, and each of its elements preserves every V_n. *Hypotheses:* k field of characteristic 0. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Jurisich 1998, Definition 4, (V1)–(V3), p. 26.)

Its API is `VertexOperatorAlgebra` (Vertex algebra with conformal vector, finite-dimensional weight spaces and weights bounded below); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.weightSpace` (The weight space V_n, n ∈ ℤ); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.finiteDimensional_weightSpace` (FiniteDimensional k (V_n)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.exists_weightSpace_eq_bot` (∃ N, ∀ n < N, V_n = ⊥); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.IsNonnegGraded` (Predicate: V_n = ⊥ for n < 0); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.IsCFTType` (Predicate: nonnegative grading, nonzero vacuum and V_0 = span{1}; in particular dim V_0 = 1. The zero vertex algebra is excluded); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.Aut` (The group of conformal automorphisms (g1 = 1, g(u_n v) = (gu)_n(gv), gω = ω)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.Aut.mapsTo_weightSpace` (g ∈ Aut maps V_n onto V_n).

*Construction.* Structure extending the vertex algebra by a conformal vector and the two finiteness conditions (FiniteDimensional k (V_n) for all n; ∃ N, ∀ n < N, V_n = ⊥). Nonnegative grading and CFT type are predicates, not fields. Conformal automorphisms preserve weight spaces because they commute with L_0 = ω_1.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.nprod` (§6.1); `ConformalVector.L`; `VertexAlgebra.Hom` (§6.1); `conformal_vector_virasoro_representation`.

**Checks.**

- A finite-dimensional commutative k-algebra with ∂ = 0 and ω = 0 is a vertex operator algebra of central charge 0 with V = V_0.
- For the lattice vertex algebra of ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2 (central charge 1), dim V_0 = 1 and dim V_1 = 3, spanned by α(−1)1, e^α, e^{−α}.
- The lattice vertex algebra of II_{1,1} with its conformal vector is not a vertex operator algebra: e^r has L_0-weight (r,r)/2 = −mn for r = (m,n), so e^{(1,n)} has weight −n (unbounded below) and V_0 contains the infinitely many independent vectors e^{(m,0)}, m ∈ ℤ.
- For a positive definite even lattice L the lattice vertex algebra satisfies IsCFTType, matching Borcherds' definition.
- The zero vertex operator algebra is nonnegatively graded and has V_0=span{0}, but is not of CFT type because its vacuum space has dimension zero.

**Invariant bilinear forms compatible with the conformal vector.** Define `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm`. Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and locally nilpotent L₁, and θ a vertex algebra automorphism of V with θ² = 1 and θ(ω) = ω (the Cartan involution; θ = id for the moonshine module). A symmetric bilinear form (·,·) on V is θ-invariant (compatible with ω in Borcherds' sense) if for every u ∈ V_i (L_0-weight i), all n ∈ ℤ and all v, w ∈ V: (u_n v, w) = (−1)^i Σ_{j≥0} (1/j!) (v, (L_1^j θ(u))_{2i−j−n−2} w). For θ = id this is the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky invariance (Y(u,z)v, w) = (v, Y(e^{zL_1}(−z^{−2})^{L_0}u, z^{−1})w). The associated contravariant form is (u, v)_0 := −(u, θ v). *Hypotheses:* V vertex algebra over k with conformal vector ω. θ ∈ Aut(V), θ² = 1, θω = ω. L₁ is locally nilpotent, so the adjoint sum terminates. This holds for a VOA whose weights are bounded below, and for lattice vertex algebras by the lower bound in each fixed lattice-degree sector; it does not follow merely from integer diagonalisation of L₀ for an arbitrary conformal vertex algebra. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Jurisich 1998, Definition 7, p. 28.)

Its API is `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm` (The predicate: B symmetric and θ-invariant in the displayed sense); `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm.adjoint_L` (B (L n v) w = B v (L (−n) w)); `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm.orthogonal_weightSpace` (B v w = 0 for v ∈ V_i, w ∈ V_j, i ≠ j); `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm.adjoint_zeroMode` (For u ∈ P^1: B (u_0 v) w = −B v ((θ u)_0 w)); `VertexAlgebra.contravariantForm` (The contravariant form (u, v)_0 := −B u (θ v)); `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm.comp_aut` (If g ∈ Aut(V, ω) commutes with θ then B(g·, g·) is again θ-invariant).

*Construction.* Define the predicate IsInvariantForm θ B by the displayed identity for homogeneous u; extend to all u by linearity using the weight decomposition. Derived properties: taking u = ω (weight 2, L_1ω = 0, θω = ω) gives L_n* = L_{−n}; taking n = −1, v = 1 gives (V_i, V_j) = 0 for i ≠ j (use L_0* = L_0); for u ∈ P^1 the formula gives u_0* = −θ(u)_0.

*Needs:* `ConformalVector.L`; `VertexAlgebra.Hom` (§6.1); Mathlib `LinearMap.BilinForm`; Mathlib `LinearMap.BilinForm.IsSymm`.

**Checks.**

- Under the stated local-nilpotence hypothesis, the zero form is invariant for every θ.
- For V_L with L even unimodular, the Fock form with (e^r, e^s) = δ_{r,s} is θ-invariant for the Cartan involution and gives (α(−1)1, β(−1)1) = ⟨α, β⟩.
- For θ = id every invariant form on V_L pairs lattice degree r only with −r; hence the Fock form (e^r, e^s) = δ_{r,s} is not id-invariant on V_L for L = ℤα, ⟨α,α⟩ = 2.
- For an invariant form, (1, v) = 0 for every v of nonzero weight.

**Conformal vector and invariant form of a tensor product.** Prove `tensor_product_conformal_structure`: Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vectors ω_V, ω_W of central charges c_V, c_W, involutions θ_V, θ_W and θ-invariant symmetric forms B_V, B_W. Then ω := ω_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ω_W is a conformal vector of V ⊗ W of central charge c_V + c_W, L_n^{V⊗W} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ L_n^W, (V⊗W)_n = ⊕_{a+b=n} V_a ⊗ W_b, θ_V ⊗ θ_W is an involution fixing ω, and B_V ⊗ B_W is a (θ_V ⊗ θ_W)-invariant symmetric form, nondegenerate when B_V and B_W are. *Hypotheses:* V, W vertex algebras with conformal vectors, involutions and invariant forms. Each factor has locally nilpotent L₁ as required by `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm`; their sum on the tensor product is locally nilpotent on each elementary tensor and finite sum. (Borcherds 1992, §3, p. 13; Jurisich 1998, §6.1, p. 30.)

*Proof sketch.* Mode formula of the tensor product: (ω_V ⊗ 1)_{n+1} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 and (1 ⊗ ω_W)_{n+1} = 1 ⊗ L_n^W; check the six conformal-vector conditions factorwise (the cross terms vanish because the two factors commute). Invariance: the adjoint formula is multiplicative for a ⊗ b with a, b homogeneous since L_1 and L_0 act as derivations of the tensor product; check on pure tensors.

*Needs:* `VertexAlgebra.tensorProduct` (§6.1); `ConformalVector.L`; `VertexAlgebra.IsInvariantForm`.

**Checks.**

- The central charge of V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} is 24 + 2 = 26 for c_V = 24.
- Borcherds 1992 §3 and Jurisich 1998 §6.1 state both parts.

**Graded trace (graded character) of an endomorphism.** Define `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace`. Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ End_k(V) with g(V_n) ⊆ V_n for all n (for example g ∈ Aut(V, ω)). The graded trace of g is Z_V(g) := Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_n) q^n ∈ k((q)) (a Laurent series because V_n = 0 for n ≪ 0). The graded dimension is Z_V(1) = Σ_n dim(V_n) q^n. Convention: no factor q^{−c/24} is included here (it is added in `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries` for c = 24). *Hypotheses:* V vertex operator algebra over k. g preserves every weight space. (Jurisich 2009, §1, p. 1; Gannon 2006, §3.1, (3.2b), p. 5.)

Its API is `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace` (Z_V(g) ∈ LaurentSeries k); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace_coeff` (coeff n (Z_V g) = tr(g|V_n)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedDimension` (Z_V(1) with coefficients dim V_n); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace_conj` (Z_V(h g h⁻¹) = Z_V(g) for h ∈ Aut(V, ω)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace_tensor` (Z_{V⊗W}(g⊗h) = Z_V(g) Z_W(h)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace_one_coeff_nonneg` (Every coefficient of the graded dimension is a natural number).

*Construction.* For each n, restrict g to the finite-dimensional V_n (LinearMap.restrict) and take LinearMap.trace; the resulting ℤ-indexed family has support bounded below, so it defines a HahnSeries ℤ k = LaurentSeries k.

*Needs:* `VertexOperatorAlgebra`; Mathlib `LinearMap.trace`; Mathlib `LaurentSeries`; Mathlib `HahnSeries`.

**Checks.**

- For the one-dimensional vertex operator algebra k (c = 0) and g = t·id, Z(g) = t.
- For the rank-one Heisenberg vertex operator algebra (lattice degree 0 part of V_{ℤα}), Z(1) = Π_{n≥1}(1 − q^n)^{−1}, with coefficients the partition numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7.
- For the involution α ↦ −α of the rank-one Heisenberg vertex operator algebra, Z(g) = Π_{n≥1}(1 + q^n)^{−1}.
- Z is not multiplicative in g: for that involution Z(g)² has q-coefficient −2 while Z(g²) = Z(1) has q-coefficient 1.

**McKay–Thompson series.** Define `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries`. Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ Aut(V, ω). The McKay–Thompson series of g is T_g := q^{−1}·Z_V(g) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_{n+1}) q^n ∈ k((q)), and c_g(n) := tr(g|V_{n+1}) (Borcherds' Thompson series Σ Tr(g|V_n)q^n with Borcherds' V_n = V_{n+1} here). The factor q^{−1} is q^{−c/24} for central charge c = 24, the case used in this layer. For a group G acting on V by conformal automorphisms, T_g for g ∈ G is a class function of g. When V is nonnegatively graded with nonzero vacuum, V_0 = k·1 and V_1 = 0, T_g = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} c_g(n) q^n. *Hypotheses:* V vertex operator algebra of central charge 24. g ∈ Aut(V, ω) (Borcherds 1992, §1, p. 2; Gannon 2006, §3.1, (3.2c), p. 5.)

Its API is `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries` (T_g := q^{−1} Z_V(g)); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries_coeff` (coeff n T_g = tr(g|V_{n+1})); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries_conj` (T_{hgh⁻¹} = T_g); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries_coeff_neg_one` (If the vacuum is nonzero and V_0=span{1}, then coeff (−1) T_g=1. Without the nonzero hypothesis the zero vertex algebra is a counterexample); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries_coeff_zero` (If V_1 = 0 then coeff 0 T_g = 0); `VertexOperatorAlgebra.mckayThompsonSeries_mul_single` (HahnSeries.single 1 1 * T_g = gradedTrace V g).

*Construction.* Define as HahnSeries.single (−1) 1 * gradedTrace V g in LaurentSeries k. The normalized shape follows from tr(g|k·1) = 1 (g1 = 1) and V_1 = 0.

*Needs:* `VertexOperatorAlgebra.gradedTrace`; `VertexOperatorAlgebra`; Mathlib `HahnSeries.single`.

**Checks.**

- For the rank-24 Heisenberg vertex operator algebra and g = 1, the coefficients of T_1 at q^{−1}, q^0, q^1, q^2 are 1, 24, 324, 3200.
- If V is nonnegatively graded then coeff n T_g = 0 for every n < −1 (T_g has at most a simple pole at q = 0).
- For the rank-24 Heisenberg vertex operator algebra, T_1 = q^{−1}Π(1−q^n)^{−24} is the q-expansion of 1/Δ, a modular form of weight −12; no constant shift of it is SL₂(ℤ)-invariant, so a McKay–Thompson series of central charge 24 need not be a modular function.
- If V is of CFT type with V_1 = 0, then T_g − q^{−1} ∈ q·k[[q]] for every g.

### 6.3 Lattice vertex algebras

**Double cover of an even lattice and its twisted group algebra.** Define `EvenLattice.Cocycle`. Let (L, ⟨·,·⟩) be an even lattice: a finitely generated free ℤ-module with a symmetric ℤ-valued bilinear form with ⟨α,α⟩ ∈ 2ℤ for all α (in Tau Ceti: the carrier of a TauCeti.IntegralLattice satisfying IsEven). A lattice cocycle is a bimultiplicative map ε : L × L → {±1} with ε(α,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2} for all α; it satisfies ε(α,β)ε(β,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}. Cocycles exist: for a ℤ-basis e_1, …, e_d put ε(e_i,e_j) = (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_j⟩} for i < j, (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_i⟩/2} for i = j, 1 for i > j, and extend bimultiplicatively. For a field k, the twisted group algebra k_ε[L] has k-basis {e^α : α ∈ L} and product e^α e^β = ε(α,β) e^{α+β}; it is associative with unit e^0. Define L̂ abstractly as {±1} × L with multiplication (s,α)(t,β) = (stε(α,β),α+β). This is a central extension 1 → {±1} → L̂ → L → 1 with commutator (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}, unique up to isomorphism; two cocycles give isomorphic twisted group algebras. The realization L̂ = {±e^α} inside k_ε[L] is faithful only if char(k)≠2. *Hypotheses:* L free of finite rank. ⟨·,·⟩ symmetric, ℤ-valued and even. (Borcherds 1986, §2, p. 2; Jurisich 1998, §6.1, p. 27.)

Its API is `EvenLattice.Cocycle` (Bimultiplicative ε : L → L → ℤˣ with ε α α = (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2}); `EvenLattice.Cocycle.exists` (Every even lattice admits a cocycle (built from a basis)); `EvenLattice.Cocycle.mul_swap` (ε α β * ε β α = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}); `EvenLattice.TwistedGroupAlgebra` (k_ε[L] is a cocycle-indexed type whose coefficients are finitely supported on L, with e^αe^β=ε(α,β)e^(α+β). The type retains ε: different cocycles cannot silently select the same untwisted multiplication instance); `EvenLattice.TwistedGroupAlgebra.single_mul_single` (e^α * e^β = ε α β • e^{α+β}); `EvenLattice.TwistedGroupAlgebra.equivOfCocycle` (Two cocycles give isomorphic twisted group algebras (by rescaling basis vectors). The cocycle comparison uses sign-valued coboundaries; no square roots of arbitrary field elements are assumed); `EvenLattice.Cocycle.orderedSign_comparison` (For an ordered ℤ-basis (b_i) of L, AffineLieAlgebras C7's ordered sign cocycle ε′(α,β) = (−1)^{Σ_{i>j}⟨b_i,b_j⟩α_iβ_j} has the same commutator (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩} but in general ε′(α,α) ≠ (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2}. With f(α) = (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2 + Σ_i (⟨b_i,b_i⟩/2)·α_i(α_i−1)/2}, the basis cocycle ε of this statement satisfies ε(α,β) = ε′(α,β)f(α)f(β)f(α+β), so e^α ↦ f(α)e^α is an algebra isomorphism k_{ε′}[L] ≅ k_ε[L]).
